speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise under the provisions of Standing Order 43 to introduce a motion on a question of urgent and pressing necessity. In view of the government's frequently stated commitment to encourage vigorous public participation on the decisionmaking processes of government and its more specific commitment to ensure that the current Mackenzie Valley pipeline hearings of the National Energy Board be open to the representations of all concerned public groups, and in view of the absolute necessity of securing as much information and as many opinions as possible relative to the social, economic and environmental impact of this critical pipeline project, I move, seconded by the hon. member for Cape Breton-East Richmond (Mr. Hogan):
That this House instruct the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources to provide all necessary financial and logistical support for all public groups wishing to participate in the current NEB hearings so that a well-informed and just decision on the proposed Mackenzie Valley Pipeline may be possible.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, under the provisions of Standing Order 43, I ask for the unanimous consent of the House to discuss a very urgent and important matter.
Considering that the Alberta tar sands will require disbursements of several billion dollars to ensure future energy supplies for the needs of the Canadian people as a whole and that these disbursements are now made on foreign financial markets, giving our natural wealth, the tar sands of Alberta, to foreigners, I move, seconded by the hon. member for Roberval (Mr. Gauthier):
That the government make all necessary arrangements to ensure that a loan trust company is established to enable all Canadians to borrow money from it to buy shares in the Alberta tar sands and also to enable Canadians to hold 51 per cent of the shares.

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I should like to direct a question to the Secretary of State for External Affairs relating to the agreement to sell a nuclear reactor to the Republic of South Korea. Will the minister, having refused to table the treaty or agreement in advance of committing Canada to the sale and to the agreement, now indicate whether Canada is insisting upon repatriation of all spent fuel in connection with this reactor, or is insisting on inspection in connection with these facilities in South Korea by Canadians in that country?

speakeroldname: Hon. Allan J. MacEachen (Secretary of State for External Affairs):
speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: EXTERNAL AFFAIRS
subsubtopic: SALE OF NUCLEAR REACTOR TO SOUTH KOREA-POSSIBILITY OF REPATRIATION OF SPENT FUEL AND INSPECTION BY CANADIANS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, we have not yet signed a nuclear co-operation agreement with the Republic of Korea. We are well on the way to entering into an agreement on nuclear co-operation but we are not insisting on the repatriation of the spent fuel because of the cost and its environmental implications to Canada, and mainly because such repatriation would not contribute significantly to safeguards in the situation we are seeking.
On the final point, I believe I am right in saying that the international agency will conduct inspections in the normal course, and that we will be considering our own inspections in respect of those aspects that are uncovered by the International Atomic Energy Agency service.

This seems like a reversal and a weakening of Canada's position. However, in connection with the discussions going on among the supplier nations, and those are the nations that supply nuclear technology and facilities, I understand there is

some kind of an agreement on common safeguards that is almost within reach. Is Canada proposing that there be IAEA inspection insisted upon by all supplier nations of not only nuclear reactors but, particularly, reprocessing facilities as well as the handling and the disposal of spent fuel?

speakeroldname: Hon. Allan J. MacEachen (Secretary of State for External Affairs):
speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: AGREEMENT AMONG SUPPLIERS OF NUCLEAR TECHNOLOGY ON SAFEGUARDS
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, at tfle meeting of the suppliers Canada is taking, and I am wondering how to put this without seeming that we are putting ourselves in a special position, an extreme position in favour of a full scope of safeguards. On a final supplementary question, Mr. Speaker, does the minister think it is appropriate for Canada to supply a nuclear reactor and nuclear fuel to a country without these general safeguards of an IAEA inspection of reactors, spent fuel and, particularly, processing facilities, in view of the fact that spent fuel developed from a Canadian reactor might very well be used in some uninspected reprocessing facility for the development of a very dangerous substance? I ask the minister whether Canada should proceed in those circumstances, and also what Canada is proposing to other nations to assist them by way of sanctions to countries which receive these nuclear facilities and do not comply with the common safeguards.

speakeroldname: Hon. Allan J. MacEachen (Secretary of State for External Affairs):
speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: GOVERNMENT POSITION ON SALE OF NUCLEAR TECHNOLOGY WITHOUT EVERY SAFEGUARD POSSIBLE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I agree with the Leader of the Opposition that it would not be appropriate for Canada to make supplies available in the circumstances he has mentioned. That is why we are, in reaching bilateral agreements with for example Argentina and the Republic of South Korea, insisting upon full safeguards with regard to inspection and reprocessing, for example, of spent fuel. We are insisting upon a Canadian hold on the uses to which spent fuel can be put and we are certainly insisting upon full inspection mainly through the International Energy Agency and in some cases it may be necessary for Canada to provide a supplementary inspection service.
So we are fully in support and are developing these inspection coverages. With regard to the final point on the sanctions, I am not aware that Canada at the present time is making any special proposals for sanctions except in the abrogation of any such bilateral or multilateral agreement. Of course, it would be open to supplier countries to cease making supplies available or to cut off all forms of nuclear co-operation which is what we have done with India but which is not fully effective.

November 4, 1975

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, as Dr. Schlesinger was a proponent of strong conventional forces as an alternative to nuclear retaliation, can the minister assure the House and the country that Dr. Schlesinger's departure will not change the Canadian Government's commitment to maintain our NATO forces in Europe at least at their present levels and that Canada will not revert to the policy of nuclear weapons as the only defence.

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I think that the policy of the United States secretary of defence, in which we believe, is that the central objective is to achieve international stability and that we achieve that stability by means of a balance of military forces and that we achieve that balance in the three areas of strategic nuclear, theatre nuclear and conventional weapons. subtopic: UNEMPLOYMENT INSURANCE ACT (1971) MEASURE TO ADD NEW CLASS OF INSURABLE EMPLOYMENT

speechtext: The House resumed, from Monday, November 3, consideration of the motion of Mr. Andras that Bill C-69, to amend the Unemployment Insurance Act, 1971, be read the second time and referred to the Standing Committee on Labour, Manpower and Immigration.

subtopic: UNEMPLOYMENT INSURANCE ACT (1971) MEASURE TO ADD NEW CLASS OF INSURABLE EMPLOYMENT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, last evening I had time for only a very brief comment before ten o'clock. It appears that views on this particular bill vary considerably and the reasons for opposing it vary considerably. I, personally, take very little pleasure in opposing this piece of legislation. Goodness knows, the act needs amending. Indeed, my main reason for opposing it is that the act needs rewriting from top to bottom. The government is once again tinkering with a piece of legislation which requires major reform.
To look at specifics, the bill claims to eliminate inequities in the existing act. I suggest that the measure before us does nothing of the kind. It does not even remove some of the minor inequities, and for every one that is perhaps eliminated two more are introduced. The bill's complexities are of the same order. According to the material provided by the minister, the bill will extend the period during which eligibility for benefit may be established in respect of persons who have left the labour force for a time for reasons beyond their control, such as disability under workmen's compensation. I am not at all sure that the provisions in the legislation will do anything to deal with some of the problems I have encountered. I am thinking in particular of a gentleman who went on workmen's compensation in September, His sixty-fifth birthday was in May of the following year. He was not interested in drawing unemployment insurance because he was receiving workmen's compensation benefits. However, there is a benefit called a three-week retirement entitlement, and he was not allowed to take advantage of this entitlement although he had contributed to the plan for 34 years.
Worse than that was the fact that when I raised the matter with the officials in the department, they twice agreed that the man was entitled to benefit yet on the third occasion turned him down again. That time, of course, they made a slip, but as a consequence this man still has no entitlement to his three-week retirement benefit.
Another gentleman because he had a younger family, continued working until he was 73 years of age. By the time he got around to retiring he knew about the three-week retirement entitlement, but was told he could not have it because he was three years past the age at which the benefits were paid. Had he quit working at 70, he could have collected his three-week benefit and then gone back to work for the next three years, with no problem. As it was, the man was disentitled from obtaining benefit, having worked even longer to pay into the plan.

One of the main features of the plan seems to be to take it out of the over 65-year olds, the contention being that the over 65s are well looked after in other ways. I think the minister is saying in this legislation that some of the over 65s have been abusing the plan. There may be some who have, as there are in any age group, but the number is minute compared to the abuses that take place in the 20 to 25 age bracket. I ask the minister why he intends to take it out of the aged. Some people in the over 65 age group are breadwinners. For various reasons they have young families; perhaps because they married a second time or adopted children. These people need to work and they want to work beyond the age of 65.
The saving that will be accomplished by taking the over 65s off the rolls will be minuscule. There are already provisions in the act to pay benefits if errors are made. We have the weird and wonderful sensation of the department from time to time trying to garnishee old age security. If errors are made, surely the department should admit they have been made, and if benefits should have been paid in the first place perhaps it is time the commission were smart enough to admit they should have been paid.
There are other amendments to the plan, including coverage under Local Initiative and Local Employment Assistance Programs. Although this is a very small item, it now seems that anyone who runs out of unemployment insurance can apply under the LIP program and get back on unemployment insurance; then the next year he can apply under the LEAP program and once more get back on unemployment insurance. I think that is the best deal yet for anyone who is a professional and not working.

subtopic: UNEMPLOYMENT INSURANCE ACT (1971) MEASURE TO ADD NEW CLASS OF INSURABLE EMPLOYMENT
speechtext: From LIP to LEAP.

subtopic: UNEMPLOYMENT INSURANCE ACT (1971) MEASURE TO ADD NEW CLASS OF INSURABLE EMPLOYMENT
speechtext:
From LIP to LEAP, with UIC in between. The government is also introducing greater flexibility into the payment of sickness benefits. This is something that needs to be done. We have all come across claimants who have been laid off during the winter time for one or two weeks. There are a number of reasons for this; for example, the owner of a small business might take a holiday so he has to lay off his employees for three or four weeks. They all draw unemployment insurance, then five or six months later the employer himself becomes seriously ill but receives no sick benefits because of his previous entitlement.
A few years ago I went into considerable detail in looking into the Unemployment Insurance Commission. Most hon. members will remember some of the situations I ran across, catalogued and presented to the House; for example, there were abuses of the plan involving some $1 billion. None of my findings was ever seriously challenged by the minister or his department, though they had the RCMP trying to find something wrong with them. One of the challenges that I issued at that time, and which I issue again now, is in the area of sick benefits. The department is well aware that errors have been made in their calculations to the tune of $250 million to $300 million, yet despite those errors in calculation the bill was allowed to proceed. These figures were never corrected, showing an arrogant and ill-disguised disregard for the people of Canada.
Four years later we are facing the same problem. But what are we doing about it? We are using a band-aid where
November 4, 1975

major surgery is required. The minister has made quite a point of saying that he is eliminating the disincentives that might be associated with the current legislation. In other words, he is saying that if workers quit then they have a six-week disentitlement. According to the information given by the minister, the number of disqualifications has not improved very much. As a matter of fact, the situation is a little worse; the number is around 300,000 annually. I suggest this number will not be changed by imposing a piddling little penalty that increases the period to six weeks. If you work for a while, then get yourself laid off or fired so as to get unemployment insurance benefits, the length of time you are off work before receiving benefits really is not that important. If you are going to milk the system, a couple of weeks one way or the other is not of much consequence.
Would it not make more sense to relate the length of the period of benefits to the work period? One of the major problems employers find today is getting decent help. I am sure there is not a member of the House who has not had this problem put to him by small businessmen who are trying to compete with unemployment insurance. I do not think I am unique, and my files are full of such cases.
One of the changes made in the legislation which seems to me almost like a damn fool clause is the provision removing from coverage persons who control 50 per cent of their own company. Frankly, these people did not want to be in the plan in the first place. I previously have spelled out to the House the case of a gentleman in the $50,000 a year bracket who successfully collected unemployment insurance for seven weeks and still drew full salary-and all of this legally, without abrogating the legislation at all.
There have been many abuses of the act, and I do not need to go into them now in detail. But the important thing is that the legislation is not going to change the situation at all. Surely, the provision regarding voluntary termination need not have been written into the act. If someone wishes for some reason or other to cease drawing benefits, surely it is not necessary to write this into the legislation.
The threshold formula, the new benchmark, is surely an admission by the government of its inability to bring unemployment down to the level it should be. The government increases the rate by 20 per cent, yet at the same time preaches restraint. It asks management and labour to hold to the 10 per cent line, then forces both into the position of paying an extra 20 per cent to the UIC.
I do not have much sympathy either for big corporations or big unions, most of which are quite capable of looking after themselves. The worry I have, and I am sure it is the worry of most members of parliament, is for small businessmen, carpenters, tradesmen who work in a very small company, people who do not have the protection of major unions or corporations to look after their needs. These big corporations, and in some cases big unions, are as much responsible for inflation as anyone else, but they run a poor second to the Government of Canada.
The increase of 20 per cent is not fair at this time. Why put it in now, particularly when the minister admitted to me in answer to a question yesterday that income is coming in faster than it is going out? Why put it in, when
Unemployment Insurance Act
the minister said-if I read his answer correctly, and I double-checked it today to make sure-the premiums collected are in fact being used not only to pay benefits but to pay back the overcharges during the past few years? The minister suggested that if this situation continues as it has in the past, there will be enough premiums collected to balance the account in the very near future. If that is the case, why do we require the extra 20 per cent right now: it only adds to the burden that labour must carry? I am as much in favour as anyone of our having an actuarially sound scheme, but in view of the way the situation appears to be developing there is no need for this increase at this time.
I see that my time has almost expired, Mr. Speaker. Unlike hon. members to my left and to my right, I do not take a great deal of pleasure in opposing this bill. I would much prefer to see the bill properly rewritten to include some of the changes suggested by my colleagues. Other hon. members have gleefully referred to some of the problems. I wish I could vote for a bill that would do the job that is necessary, but as I see it the minister is still deceiving the Canadian public by telling them that this measure is necessary to solve our unemployment insurance problems. What we need is some basic honesty in this or some other piece of legislation to correct the Unemployment Insurance Act. I would gladly support such a piece of legislation.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I take the opportunity of this debate on second reading of Bill C-69 to say a few words about the unemployment insurance program. Although the bill deals with specific amendments, it is normal, at this stage of the discussions, to talk about the whole program.
I support the motion that the bill be referred to the Standing Committee on Labour, Manpower and Immigration because I think that it has been sufficiently improved to be submitted to the consideration of the committee where the members will proceed to a thorough study.
However, I will make a few reservations later with respect to this bill.
I congratulate the minister for the amendments pertaining to old age and maternity insurance, which have already been passed pursuant to another bill. As for the entitlement of LIP sponsors, the legislation will enable applicants to discontinue voluntarily the benefits and provide for the extension of the qualifying period as well as for the eligibility of claimants who are in receipt of workmen's compensation payments, of prisoners and other workers who had to quit their jobs for reasons beyond their control.
I think these amendments are wise and will result in a better program. The minister listened carefully to the debate and I hope he will be convinced of the value of amending the bill. In my view, we should not start disqualifying any claimant from the unemployment insurance program, nor should we delete any item from the program, which may result in making it less liberal, until a comprehensive survey of all our social and economic adjustment programs has been carried out. An attempt should be made to merge those programs one way or another and perhaps it could be useful to have a parliamentary committee consid-

er the suggestion. At one point, Mr. Speaker, I thought of introducing an amendment to that motion which would precisely have the effect of withdrawing the bill and referring its subject matter to a committee. But I see that such an act on my part, if my amendment were accepted, would seriously delay the passage of the good aspects of the bill.
So I thought it might be better if I joined others of my colleagues and opposition members to try and improve the bill at the committee stage or the report stage. However, I will continue to make that suggestion before we make other minor changes at random in the unemployment insurance program, those changes will not be an improvement but a departure from the program we had in 1971. I will continue to make the suggestion to try and get terms of reference for a parliamentary committee so hon. members may examine the variety of our programs and our policy of economic and social changes so we can, at least at the conceptual level, merge some of those programs and have a much more rational approach that would meet most of the recognized disadvantages of the program and the criticisms we hear in this House or elsewhere.
I think all participants in this debate agree on certain points of the unemployment insurance program. I see a common denominator on many factors. First, all those who spoke in this debate agree that we need an unemployment insurance program, a work insurance program. Second in amending the legislation all want as much as possible to stop abuses in the unemployment insurance program. Third, they want our social programs to encourage productivity, and when I use the word "productivity" I do not mean mere economic productivity, but social and economic productivity.
I really think that parliamentary committee could make a non-partisan and in-depth study and arrive at recommendations that would improve our social programs. Hon. members can assess those programs because they know the problems. There are few of their offices where the staff is not constantly urged to intervene with the Unemployment Insurance Commission, or the provincial social service departments, on behalf of the unemployed or those who feel ill-treated by the civil service or by the programs themselves.
To my mind, this Bill C-69 goes too far on the one hand, and not far enough on the other. Still, I can understand that the minister intended to bring in changes at this time, that he had reasons to wait-as he mentioned in his speech-for a far more complete and comprehensive revision. As regards the change in the legislation aiming at solving the problem of voluntary retirement from work through legislative means, I think that we should try to solve this problem through administrative means. I admit that it is important for some people to put it into the act, but in my opinion this problem can be solved through administrative improvements. It is not necessary to amend the act, but on this point I can say that personally I would rather not see this amendment in the bill, although I can accept it, precisely because I think it is an administrative problem.
If a recipient cannot prove that he is actively seeking employment, he is disqualified for an indefinite period. So what then is the solution of the proposed amendment? Nothing, from a legislative point of view, because with a

good administration, a humane administration of course, good results can be achieved. By the way, I might say that the administration of the Unemployment Insurance Commission is improving, at least in my region. We have had problems when the two programs were combined, the one before 1971 and the new one, but I can say that in my region, and I think that it is the same in the Atlantic region in general, the administration of the program is improving as regards efficiency and that it is becoming more humane following the changes made last year.
Thus we can now eliminate indefinitely, and not only for three or six weeks, those who are not actively looking for a job.
Unfortunately, the bill ventures into two other areas concerning the philosophy of the program and, as I said earlier, I think the government should steer clear of a piecemeal approach toward important programs like the unemployment insurance scheme before a study is made on the whole situation. I hope that before proceeding to his new series of amendments, the minister will ensure that a parliamentary committee, and I insist on this, makes a study on the subject. I insist on this because, through the very nature of their work and through their participation in society, hon. members know the problems of social adjustment and of poverty in general, and I would like to have a parliamentary study on the subject.
Those two provisions which I would have preferred to see deferred are the lowering from 70 to 65 of the maximum age for coverage under the plan. I said earlier that I would support the motion for second reading of the bill, but I wish to tell the House and the minister that I am against the change in maximum age for coverage. I will oppose it in committee if I get a chance, and I will oppose it in the House if amendments are moved; moreover, I might move some myself. I also oppose another proposed change in the rate of benefits for claimants with dependents. I understand the arguments of the minister in favour of both of these changes. I agree that, had we introduced those changes when we increased old-age pensions and modified the family allowance plan, it might not have been possible then.
I agree in principle that the Unemployment Insurance Plan should not normally be used in that way, since it is a problem which will have to be dealt with in another program. Unfortunately, timing is important when dealing with government affairs, and I do not think we should start denying anyone benefits unless we clearly have something else to offer. I might agree to those changes later, when we have carried out a more detailed study of the matter as the minister mentioned, with a view to bring all social programs into line. Perhaps then we will be in a position to come up with an evaluation. But right now, I object to those measures. This, however, is no reason for opposing the second reading of the bill, which contains some good provisions. I think we all agree with some of the amendments proposed in the bill. I do not think it would be reasonable to oppose it on second reading. But later, when it comes to third reading, unless those measures are modified, I will find it extremely difficult to support the bill.
November 4, 1975

I would like to deal very briefly with some of the arguments that have come forward concerning the philosophy of the program. I said earlier I would agree to a basic and comprehensive reform not only of the unemployment insurance program but also the economic and social adjustment program of the government. I think a parliamentary study of this problem would be useful. The minister in his speech mentioned that he is conducting a review of the UIC program. I should like to quote the minister in order to put in proper context what I am saying. As reported at page 8567 of Hansard, the minister said:
I should like to emphasize that the changes contained in this bill which is being presented to parliament are the results of the first findings of our review of the legislation. However, as is proper with a program of such significance, this comprehensive examination is continuing, particularly in relationship to two parallel policy developments. I mentioned one, the over-all harmonization of all our social security programs. The other is the evolution of an integrated and more comprehensive manpower policy.
I was glad to hear the minister say those words. He has shown in the past that he is the type of man who would be very co-operative. I am sure he will consider favourably my suggestion that once we have dealt with this bill, in conjunction with the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Lalonde) he conduct a review of all these programs, not only UIC. In my view, it has to do with all social and economic adjustment programs.
Given the fact that unemployment is a reality in this country, primarily it is a regional problem. I have always said that one day I would like to make a special study in this regard, and probably I will. I would like to know exactly what the impact of unemployment is on the Gaspe peninsula, the northern region of Quebec, the northern region of New Brunswick, Newfoundland, and a few other regions of the country. I should like to see exactly what impact national unemployment has on employment situation in these regions. Perhaps we are not talking about an employment problem or a social adjustment problem at all but, rather, a regional economic problem.
That is the reason I would like to see some kind of approach adopted that would try to merge the unemployment insurance program with the local Employment Assistance Program-which is a wonderful program-the Local Initiatives Program, the Canada Assistance Plan and even some DREE agreements. There is a DREE agreement in my constituency-a FRED agreement. We are initiating discussions to renew it under the present development agreement. Really, we are dealing with social adjustment and not only economic development. It has been proven now that industrialization is not the only answer to economic development. We will have to look at other things.
I should like to say briefly that I cannot agree with those on the opposite side, both Progressive Conservatives and members of the New Democratic Party, who say it is a terrible thing to change the threshold of 4 per cent unemployment to a given average of unemployment in the pre-vions eight years. To me, it does not make very much difference when one considers that contributions are tax deductible and that some people who pay income tax into the consolidated revenue fund have no relationship at all
Unemployment Insurance Act
to employment. I refer to retired people and people with savings who pay income tax.
People, particularly members of the New Democratic Party, raise the fundamental problem of the employer and the worker contributing to the program, versus the consolidated or general revenue of the government. When one balances this argument, I do not see that it matters. One could take the position that the unemployment insurance program is primarily for workers and employers, and that probably they should pay for the administration of the program in order to receive benefits under it.
I can see, on the other hand, having the threshold, the principle we introduced in 1971, because there is a degree of incentive on the general economy and the government to try to lower unemployment. I have listened very carefully to the debate, all the arguments made by members of the New Democratic Party and some from the official opposition, but I am not convinced that this is a serious problem. I can live with that part of the bill.
I repeat, I regret that in starting our review of the Unemployment Insurance Act we have to hurt some people. I know the minister to be a reasonable and flexible man. I hope he has listened to and appreciated the concern of members from all sides of the House, on two questions particularly. One is the reduction of the age of eligibility from 70 to 65 and the other concerns doing away with the special allocation to claimants who are dependents. I sincerely hope the minister will see fit to accept amendments in the committee or in the House when the bill comes back here.
In conclusion, I would like to say that I am one of those who is not very impressed with some of the arguments we hear, particularly from some members of the official opposition. We are lucky there are members from the Atlantic provinces in that party, as well as from other regions, who-probably for regional reasons, if one can call them that, because their constituents are mainly people of low income, working people-bring some reason to the debate. I have been concerned since 1971, and was in the 1972 campaign-the same arguments are being advanced again now, probably because of events coming up in February in the Conservative party-that the unemployment insurance program is a mess and that it will cost $3.6 billion compared to the many hundreds of millions of dollars which it cost before 1971.
I should like to say first of all to people who put forward this cost argument-the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Stanfield) was one of those who advanced this argument last week in another debate-that they are not completely honest because they are comparing apples with oranges. The fact is that we are not dealing with the same program at all. Before 1971 there was no provision for sickness in the unemployment insurance program, no provision for maternity benefits, and the income tax was not recoverable. So we are not talking about $3.6 billion. Even if the amount is high-I have said this before in the House-I do not know why people become so upset when governments intervene in society and in the economy. I am surprised, because those who argue against government spending, against social subsidies-unemployment insurance is one

November 4, 1975
Unemployment Insurance Act
of them-are the very people who benefit from higher technology and higher productivity brought about through these various adjustment programs. They are the very same people, from the same regions and the same sectors of this society.
I have heard people from the Canadian Chamber of Commerce, the Canadian Manufacturers' Association and the business community complain in private about the terrible unemployment insurance program which is costing so much money and which, in their words, is a disincentive to work. In fact, they are the people who need this program, because without good social and economic adjustment programs, which really the Unemployment Insurance Act is, there would be reluctance from communities and from provincial and municipal governments to change. There would also be reluctance from workers and labour unions to technological change.
I have given examples previously of projects which have gone ahead which are in the long-term interest of the nation or of a particular region, but which in the process of increasing productivity and technological advancement have required the dislocation of people. When you dislocate people, you need some kind of adjustment program. The people who benefit from higher productivity and technology have to pay for those who are dislocated-and who will do that, if not the government?
Therefore, it seems to me that the search to be more competitive in the world, more technologically advanced and more productive, is compatible with high government spending on social intervention programs, because without these programs there would be reluctance from the different segments of society. Unless people who advance these arguments want to suggest that we adopt a kind of system that would force people to do things and ignores pressures in society against change, I cannot see that they are serious.
With regard to this program being a disincentive to work, I do not believe that in today's society we can say that generally speaking the unemployment insurance program is a disincentive to work. I admit that there are abuses of the program. I have seen cases of such abuses and I deplore them, but I say that with good administration and a human approach we can deal with these problems. Before concluding I would like to make one point, namely, that the unemployment insurance program is not the only government program where abuses exist. There are abuses in any public program, abuses of the income tax system and of other programs, so this is not the only program in which abuses exist.
With regard to the argument that it is bad to have working people off work for a certain period of time, let me point out that working people are not the only people off work for part of the year. I know of people in the professions, people from the business world who spend two or three months a year in Florida or in California. They are not very productive there. If they can earn enough in six or nine months to be able to go elsewhere for the rest of the year, or if they can play golf half the time in the summer, then I am happy for them. What is the difference if it is the working people who are doing this? The only difference is that if the working people do this, if they are off the job

and are not being productive for a certain part of the year, the only recourse for them is a public program.
I would not like to hear anyone argue that the working people or people who are unemployed are the only ones who are not productive the year round. Other people in society are not productive the year round, and I am not suggesting that they should be. Some people can earn a very high income for six or nine months of the year and then be off for the other three months. If some people, because of the geography of this country, because of their particular region, the nature of the economy in that region or the nature of the industry where they work, happen to be unemployed for part of the year, I do not see why it is worse than having people from other classes in society take off for part of the year.
I will watch very closely what goes on in committee with this bill, and I will watch very closely what happens in the House when it comes back here. I have mentioned that there are two provisions I cannot support, but I will not vote against the second reading motion because I believe the bill should go forward, having, as it does, some good provisions in it. As I said a short while ago, unless these two provisions are changed I will find it very difficult to support the bill. But I will see what developments take place in committee. I have been in the House for seven or eight years; that is long enough to know that one should not become concerned about the future before it comes around. We will cross those bridges when we come to them.
I hope the minister will seriously consider my suggestions. I suggest to him, again, that a parliamentary committee should receive a reference from the House to study the whole spectrum of social and economic adjustment programs in order to see how the programs in place are functioning. He has spoken about the harmonization of our social programs. I believe that either a joint committee or a House committee should receive a reference from the House to study this whole problem before the minister proceeds with a second review of the unemployment insurance program, because this act is a crucial element of our social security programs and it also has implications in respect of economic adjustment, not only social adjustment.

subtopic: UNEMPLOYMENT INSURANCE ACT (1971) MEASURE TO ADD NEW CLASS OF INSURABLE EMPLOYMENT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, like others in the House, I welcome the opportunity to express my views on Bill C-69 and the Unemployment Insurance Commission which, after all, is an institution with which all of us as parliamentarians have had many dealings. It is, therefore, with great pleasure that I take this opportunity to speak on it because I believe a discussion in the House on this subject is long overdue. Happily, the Unemployment Insurance Commission has managed to serve a need in difficult times, and for this we can all be grateful. However, because of its structure under existing law it has also created new sets of mores and attitudes, many of which I find rather frightening.
There are frightening financial implications as well. Let us consider the figures for the 30 years between 1940 and 1970. Unemployment costs for those years were something of the order of $6 billion, whereas in the last four years the cost of financing this institution, or unemployment costs, were of the order of $10 billion. In other words, 30 years, $6 billion; 5 years, $10 billion. The Unemployment Insurance
November 4, 1975

Commission is a controversial institution, and therefore this debate is most welcome. Of course, I shall only be able to address myself to certain elements but I hope that in the course of this debate and in committee some of these matters may be resolved.
There is no question in my mind that even in its present form the Unemployment Insurance Commission serves a need, because we can all recognize that we have a regrettably high degree of unemployment, and for those who are unable to find employment the commission offers temporary financial assistance for qualified workers. Unfortunately, sometimes it also offers assistance of more than a temporary nature for workers who may be qualified but who are unwilling to rejoin the labour force. This assistance is offered on such a scale that the disincentive to rejoin the labour force can become extraordinarily high. I say this for good reason. Despite the high rate of unemployment there are many opportunities for work in this country. This is still a country of opportunity.
Figures are not easily come by, but I did manage to find some. In a period of high unemployment the Victoria, British Columbia, Canada Manpower office was indicating, on a long roll of paper, that there were 1,132 vacancies in the area. This was in June of 1973. I do not have comparable figures for people receiving unemployment insurance benefits. This was a chance release in the newspaper. These were not all specialized jobs; the list comprised skilled and unskilled jobs, marine draughtsmen, psychiatric nurses, medical technologists, legal stenographers, secretaries, accountants, bookkeepers, automatic transmission specialists, and bricklayers. Even when people are on unemployment insurance benefits there are many jobs available, and this is an aspect which I find a little frightening. I shall be returning to this point and seeking ways to overcome this shortcoming of the present organization.
In this context, I welcome the statements and thoughts expressed by my hon. friend opposite, the hon. member for Gloucester (Mr. Breau), who said that he would like to see a study of all the social security programs or, as he calls them, the social adjustment programs, to see if out of it cannot be made an amalgam. However, I shall be returning to this matter before the end of my comments. I leave it to others in this debate-some have already done so; some, no doubt, will turn to it again-to underline the financial consequences to our society of having to face the monumental cost of financing the operations of the commission.
I have mentioned the scale of those costs. There are provisions in the amendments to reduce, at least to some extent, the charges which will fall upon the Canadian public. These operations, however, have consequences other than the financial ones, having equally frightening effects on the social fabric of our nation such as destroying or at least wearing down the urge to work, which was denied by the previous speaker but which I insist does exist. By wearing down the urge to work and to retain one's independence of action, we accept slavery and dependence on the state for all our being's needs, wants and fulfilment. That sterile prospect is too frightening to contemplate. We must stop that trend before it overwhelms us.
Unemployment Insurance Act
I am led to make these comments because indisputably there are a large number of unfilled jobs in this country at a time when there is rising unemployment. The phenomenon cannot be explained in any other way. Those who are out of work either do not want to fill the jobs available, or are perhaps refusing to seek retraining which would prepare them to do so, because of the comfortable haven offered by unemployment insurance benefits. If this practice continues unabated it can lead to social bankruptcy and economic disaster.
This automatically brings us to the role the Manpower offices play in restoring this matter to equilibrium. On good authority I have been informed that one Manpower officer has tossed out, without too much show of concern, the fact that in the 17 years he has been employed at a Manpower centre-presumably to find employment for others and safely employ himself-he has not placed a single person in a job. In the sharpest and cruellest light, this comment underlines one great defect in the unemployment picture in Canada today: the failure of the unemployment offices and Manpower centres to work as one service-first, to take care of those in financial need and, second, to meet the employment need. It should be one service. In various locations in cities which I know there is rivalry between the two services. Refusal to accept an employment offer or a reasonable offer of retraining-and they can be equated-ought to be a cause to have the individual concerned removed from the insurance rolls.
Contrary to what has been said by some whom I have thought to be reliable spokesmen, the unemployment insurance system in Canada is not, I insist, one of the means by which the wealth of the nation is to be more equally distributed. To my way of thinking, that is not the purpose of unemployment insurance. If that is what the law is doing, then the law must be changed. An unemployment insurance fund should be an insurance fund to insure against the financial consequences of economic adversity which any one of us can meet. We should all be prepared to say, "There, but for the grace of God, go I." The insurance fund is there to help those of us who are in need; it is not for the redistribution of the wealth of this country. It is called an insurance fund and that is the role it should play, not any other.
I should like to get into a little more of the philosophy which ought to motivate the commission in its handling of a serious socioeconomic problem. I may do so, if time permits, at the conclusion of my other comments. Incidentally, I seem to have forgotten to look at the time I started my speech and I shall therefore rely on the Chair to remind me when my time begins to expire.
I should like to discuss the criteria for entitlement, such as total family income. I should like, also, to deal with seasonal workers, as well as with long time employment as deserving special consideration under the act. However, I shall have to leave these considerations to others, since my time is limited.
My principal concern today is the deleterious effect on Canada as a whole of the deterioration of the work ethic which unemployment insurance benefits promote or foster. It is a very fine point whether they promote or foster it; in

November 4, 1975
Unemployment Insurance Act
any event, they do nothing to halt it. I want to put forward some notion about how the whole process could be reversed so that the very existence of unemployment insurance benefits would prompt people to spend less time drawing benefits.
In this connection, I was delighted last evening to hear my friend and colleague, the hon. member for Cumber-land-Colchester North (Mr. Coates), explain his views about combining certain features of the social security system. I have already mentioned that I welcomed the comments of the hon. member for Gloucester who immediately preceded me in this debate. It is my desire to see several features of our social security system and our social adjustment programs brought together, but first I think it is worth recording a bit of history.
As long ago as 1948-49, the Progressive Conservative party developed a multifaceted scheme of social security. This involved a consolidation or a combination of schemes then in existence or on the horizon. Today, as we see the variety of schemes designed for the security of the citizens working out their fate, we think the time has come-as the hon. member for Gloucester said-to revive that consolidated program or something like it. Its implementation would remove the tremendous financial burden under which federal budgets now labour in meeting the high cost of unemployment. But equally important, its implication would restore that vigorous independence that so distinctively marked an earlier generation of Canadians.
Earlier this year, in a report entitled "Canadian Work Values'' issued by the Department of Manpower and Immigration, we find the following comment:
Clearly, Canadians are committed to work ... Canadians see themselves as industrious people to whom work contributes a feeling of success and, for a large proportion, of personal fulfilment.
This "motherhood" statement was obviously verbalized in order to provide comfort and gratification to those who feel that in the Manpower section of the department, at least, they have a sense of personal fulfilment. That sort of self-adulation and self-congratulation is dangerous, Mr. Speaker. It leads to complacency and that is something we can do without at any time in our lives, but at this time particularly.
If only I could convince myself that all Canadians and all draft-dodging immigrants, if I may bring them into the picture, merited that form of compliment, I would be happy. But we must consider that a good number of the LIP grant applicants dream up their projects with two objectives in mind:-to get in on some of the fresh bread that is lying around, and to build up some credit, saying to themselves, "Let's hope we can keep the projects stalled for at least eight weeks," which would entitle them to unemployment insurance benefits after their LIP bread is used up. When I consider this, I question the smugness of such self-comforting phrases as those contained in the report.
Of course, many of our farmers, independent businessmen and other working Canadians are committed to work; they are not committed to unemployment insurance. But far too many other Canadians are, and many of them are proud of it. I do not like to hear people boasting about being able to get on to the unemployment insurance rolls

and I do not suppose anyone in this House does. This is where a great deal of danger lies, and we must overcome it.
If I could return to the consolidated scheme advanced by my party some 30 years ago, I should like to explain some of its features and the solutions it would provide to the problems I have been discussing. The proposal was based on the following schemes then more or less in operation or in contemplation: the unemployment insurance scheme, a hospitalization plan, a medicare plan and the old age pension scheme. There was an accident program thrown in for good measure, but I think we will just deal with those four.
The philosophy underlying this consolidated program was based on the notion that these four schemes could be united under one single scheme, with a single contribution for each Canadian, and placed on an actuarial footing. It was also based on the observable fact, a fact that could be proven statistically, that the generality of Canadians seldom or never, in normal circumstances, have cause to rely on unemployment insurance benefits, are seldom, or for very short periods only, obliged to go into hospital, and only a bit more frequently have to come under the medicare plan. A good many Canadians are healthy people and do not have to call on these plans but contribute to them gladly.
It is surprising, when one looks back on one's own life, just how little one has needed these services. I count myself lucky, fortunate perhaps, and I do not in the least mind paying my insurance premiums because it is comforting to know that the service is there if it should ever be needed. Unemployment, hospitalization and doctor's care were the main schemes. The actuarial tables, based on reliable statistics at that time, demonstrated that a normal healthy Canadian, making his contribution throughout his working life to this consolidated scheme and looking forward to an old age pension-at that time, munificently set at $100 a month-because he had not called on the unemployment insurance scheme, the hospital scheme or medicare to any great extent, would find his old age pension increased by about $150. This comes back to the age 65 limit that was being put on it. If a man was paying all his life to age 65 and not drawing benefits during those years, why should he not get them at that age?
