speechtext:
You try finding work at that age. The underlying theory is that to the extent that there was no call on the services available, their end of work pension or old age pension will be increased. When this was first explained to me, it was quite a new concept. I am surprised that parliament did not get down to it earlier. I do not know what happened. I think perhaps 1961-62 came along and the Liberal government decided that anything devised by the Conservatives was not worth considering. But it is there, Mr. Speaker; it is a sensible program and it would meet some of the problems now before us. It would get people off unemployment insurance and out looking for a job simply because at the end of their life they would enjoy those benefits. They would want to work in order to enjoy those benefits later. This is the great extractor of the disincentive that is causing so much concern, and has caused so much concern, to this government.
November 4, 1975

The consolidated scheme was found to be actuarially sound in 1949 when it was devised by a professor from the University of British Columbia. It was updated and found to be sound in the 1959-60 era by the government of the right hon. member for Prince Albert (Mr. Diefenbaker). It would obviously take a number of years to put into place the machinery for establishing such a comprehensive program today. It could be done. As I say, however, the scheme is there and it is an answer to the work disincentive.
The unemployment insurance program must not become another welfare program. I have said it before and it cannot be too frequently or too forcefully said. It is an insurance program, as are the hospital insurance and medical insurance schemes. Canadians can be prudent. They want to look after their own needs in these areas and will do so much more satisfactorily, and at less cost to other taxpayers, if provided with the right kind of program and the right kind of leadership which, regrettably, we lack today. I submit that the consolidated program briefly outlined is just such a program. It remains to be seen whether this government will respond to the call of the hon. member for Gloucester and other hon. members to look into the possibility of improving not only the unemployment insurance program but the other social programs available to Canadians.
There are some elements in this bill which are commendable. However, it is a patchwork exercise. In parts, it is even offensive. It leaves aside those who have reached the age of 65, denying them an entitlement to draw unemployment insurance benefits which they might otherwise have had. The amendments put forward here merely paste over cracks. The worst feature is the debilitating effect that an even more inefficient Manpower or job-creation scheme is having on Canadian society. Something much more fundamental is needed than this bill provides. At the very least, the unemployment and job-creation aspects of government programs must be brought more closely together. Better still, we should get some hint that the whole welfare scheme will be overhauled along the lines I have suggested. Until that is done we are in grave danger of social disaster, with the working majority carrying throughout their working lives the non-working minority. The Canadian public is thoroughly fed up with piggy-backing in this way.
We may be hewers of wood and drawers of water, but we will not willingly become draught animals as well, drawing after us a small but ever-growing group of people who have latched on to a good thing, a scheme which offers them greater financial return than they are prepared to look for in the labour market. It is obviously not possible to shift the Unemployment Insurance Commission into this area of reform within the terms of the present bill. I should like to leave my comments on that for a moment. There is one particular case that I feel is worth recounting for the record, in the hope that it will be remedied by different rulings than those which have prevailed.
We have all had experience with the Unemployment Insurance Commission. We have all had constituents come to us with their problems, their disentitlements, their being cut off benefits, and their failure to qualify. Even if
Unemployment Insurance Act
our debating time were not now restricted there would be insufficient time for each of us to document all of these problems. There is one, however, I wish to speak about.
The circumstances in this case were that the worker delayed her application for benefits until the exact period of her absence could be accurately determined. She was expecting a baby and wanted to receive the maternity benefits. She might, within her rights, have applied earlier but she did not. This proved her downfall because before she did file her application the municipal employees, of whom she was one, were locked out as a result of the activity of other workers. She was not directly involved in the negotiating argument that led to the lock-out, but once locked out she was considered as though she were on strike and, in consequence, not eligible for benefits.
I insist that this was a miscarriage of justice, a faulty judgment on the part of the official. I referred it to the minister and received some specious replies. Surely, some distinction ought to be made between a person who is disqualified on account of being on strike and a person who is disqualified because, through no fault of her own, she is unable to report for work. The doors were locked; she could not get in the front door. Why should she be disentitled? The doors were locked against her because others had threatened to go on strike and the lock-out occurred.
In summary, I have managed to mention the disincentives inherent in the unemployment insurance system as it now stands. I look for improvements. I have mentioned the need for closer integration between the Unemployment Insurance Commission and the Manpower centres. I managed, within my time, to cite one instance that has really bothered me. It has been the basis for a good many exchanges with the minister. I hope it will be settled, even retroactively. I know that I can count on a sympathetic hearing.

subtopic: UNEMPLOYMENT INSURANCE ACT (1971) MEASURE TO ADD NEW CLASS OF INSURABLE EMPLOYMENT
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, it is fascinating to follow this debate. Some hon. members have complained that the act and its application are too lenient, that it lends itself to so-called abuses and should be tightened up either administratively or by law. Others approached it on the basis of their own experience and the requirements of the people they represent, asking that it be made more generous and that it take into consideration factors that at present the law does not. Some members have tried to be on both sides of the fence in the same speech, arguing on either side. I suppose that is human nature. In an effort to find a better answer, everyone approaches it in what they think is the best possible way. However, surely it would help if there was a certain degree of consistency. The question is, what do we want this act to be? Do we want it to be an insurance scheme, as proposed by the hon. member for Esquimalt-Saanich (Mr. Munro), or do we want it to be an income support scheme?
Those of us who were in this House in 1971 will remember the debates at that time. We knew then, as we know today, that we were about to introduce a system of income support, not a system of insurance but a social program- not just a businessman's program, as some Tory spokesmen would like it to be. Not all of them are in agreement, I am sure. I imagine that a few minutes from now the hon. member for Cape Breton-The Sydneys (Mr. Muir), who

November 4, 1975
Unemployment Insurance Act
represents an industrial riding, will speak strongly in favour of the approach we have adopted, namely, and income support approach, because this is a good sheme, a good law.
Let us not try to make law by legislating with an eye only to abuses. If we, as legislators, were to do that we would be acting as administrators, losing sight of the general approach, a philosophy toward social legislation. We could then become civil servants administering the act and, surely, we ought not to be performing the second role; that is not our task.
Like other legislation, the bill before us today has good features, bad features and technical features. The trouble with this legislation is that it contains some very bad features. First, though, I will deal briefly with the good ones. There is a proposal for an amendment making sponsors of LIP of LEAP projects eligible for coverage. There is a provision allowing claimants to terminate their claims should they wish to do so; at present the law does not permit them to do so. There is a proposal for an extension of the period during which sickness benefits will be paid. The period is 29 weeks at present and it is be extended to 39 weeks.
There is to be an extension of the period during which uninsurable earnings may be counted for entitlement to benefit, from the present 52 weeks to 104 weeks. This amendment probably stems from proposals made in various private bills brought forward in the House from time to time during the past few years. Injured workers, exinmates of prisons and persons handicapped because of illness will benefit from this measure.
I commend the minister for having incorporated in the bill propositions which have been advanced by members from both sides of the House in the past three years. Further, it is made clear that a worker who receives workmen's compensation payments is entitled to receive benefits. As the wording presently reads, he is not entitled to do so even though he might receive compensation for one day only. The law is to be clarified to permit a person in receipt of workmen's compensation to receive benefits from unemployment insurance for parts of a week.
We are also asked to approve a measure to increase premiums paid by employers and employees. This was a responsible decision made necessary by the requirements of the program itself. I support it, as I am sure most hon. members do.
I shall not deal with the technical features of the bill. Instead, I shall consider briefly the bad features, the ones which seem, to me, to be of a negative character. There is a proposal in the legislation to reduce the present special benefit rate of 75 per cent paid to unemployed people with dependants to a level of 66 percent of their normal earnings. The consequence, I suppose, will be that in the rural or poorer areas of Canada where there is a high and constant level of unemployment, people so affected will be obliged to turn for help to provincial and municipal welfare arrangements. The onus will be shifted to other levels of government, though in the end, I suppose, it will still be a federal responsibility, indirectly, if payments are made through the Canada Assistance Plan to which we contrib-

ute to the extent of 50 per cent. It seems to me that this measure is not a good one; it will hit particularly hard the areas I have mentioned and it will hurt people whose level of income is already amoung the lowest. I would ask the minister to reconsider this proposal when the bill is before the committee.
Another bad feature has to do with the treatment of workers aged 65 and over. Take the case of men and women in our society who marry late in their lives, in their fifties, form families and are deeply interested in gainful employment for the maintenance of their families when they reach age 65 or over. If the proposed amendment is carried, we shall be treating workers aged 65 and over in a manner different from that in which we treat workers younger than 65. We shall be saying to them: You have old age security coming to you, and that should be adequate to cover your needs, whether you become unemployed or not.
Madam Speaker, we do not put forward that argument when we consider the treatment of widows and widowers below the age of 65 who receive a pension under the Canada Pension Plan and who wish to be active in the labour force. Yet we apply this type of reasoning to people aged 65 and over. I believe that in a system such as ours- undoubtedly one of the best in the world-there should be no obstacle in the way of a man or a woman who wishes to remain in the labour force, no matter what the age might be. If this premise were accepted, it would follow that entitlement under the unemployment insurance system should be the same for them as for others. There should be consistency. The drawing of a line at a certain age is completely artificial and is most frustrating to elderly people who wish to remain productive members of our society. It introduces a double standard of treatment which I do not think is a good idea.
I should like to move on to another aspect that I discussed in this House at the time of the budget. It has to do with the proposed amendment to the act that would impose a double disqualification on workers dismissed for misconduct. I ask the House, who is going to define the word "misconduct"? Will it be the employer? Will it be the unemployment insurance official? Or will it be the board of referees? It is true that when the minister spoke last week we were assured there is ample jurisprudence on the question of misconduct. Nevertheless, how are we going to apply and administer a law with a definition of "misconduct" that is so broad, that is so much left in the hands of those who will have to interpret the legislation? Surely, in the eyes of a worker "misconduct" means something quite different from what it means to an employer. What may be an offence to an employer may, in the eyes of a worker, be an insignificant pattern of behaviour.
One needs only to speak to people engaged in an assembly line operation, say, in the automotive industry, people who work under considerable tension and strain, to discover that their pattern of behaviour may be quite difficult to understand from the point of view of management. At times, such behaviour could be interpreted as misconduct. But who is to decide on a worker fired for misconduct? I regret to say that I find this proposed amendment to be one that treats workers like school children. It is like the state entering the work place and trying
November 4, 1975

to determine who is behaving well and who is not. I am not saying we are going too far; I am saying that this is an area we should not even touch.
It seems to me that these three areas do not require amendment. Where we do need amendment is, first of all, in shifting the emphasis from unemployment to employment. I should like to give the House an example that occurred in the great city of Toronto from which I come, which was reported by Wilfred List in the Globe and Mail a couple of weeks ago. The headline of his article is "29 zoo workers ignore layoff, want to work for UIC benefits". Stated simply, 29 employees of the metro zoo expressed their intention to carry out their regular duties and be ready for work for unemployment insurance benefits of $100 a week, to which they would normally be entitled. This arose out of a decision by the Toronto Zoological Society to lay off 49 employees.
Mr. Patrick O'Keeffe, the representative of CUPE to which the zoo workers belonged, sent a telegram to the minister on behalf of the workers. In the telegram he asked that the workers be paid unemployment insurance while they continued to do necessary work at the zoo without salary. The relevant question is this, as asked by Mr. O'Keeffe: "If they are going to give them $100 a week for idling, why not for voluntary, necessary labour?" This is why I say we need amendments that shift the emphasis from unemployment to employment, amendments that would permit using unemployment insurance funds to design and to create jobs.
Secondly, we need amendments that will shift the emphasis from inactivity to training. To some extent we have already done this. The minister has initiated some interesting examples of this on a small scale in Newfoundland. Unemployed workers there were given, in addition to their regular Manpower allowance, a UIC allowance, to top it all, while in training. We need amendments to apply this approach to the whole country and make it possible for those who become unemployed but who wish to work and upgrade themselves to utilize the period they are unemployed constructively and purposefully both with regard to the present and the future.
Thirdly, we need amendments of a day to day nature, particularly in our large cities, which will permit people no longer unemployed to deal with the commission. For example, the office should be open evenings so that a person who has found employment can settle a claim. People should be able to telephone the commission in the daytime and get through to the officer in charge of their claim, which is not possible now in Toronto-and, I suspect, in other cities too-so as to clean up their case by telephone instead of being required to attend at the office personally.
Lastly, we should extend into the evening hours the hearings of the board of referees. Why should the operations of the commission be oriented to the convenience of the commission? Why cannot operations be oriented to the convenience of the users, particularly those users who, through their own efforts or with the help of government services, have managed to become employed again? Surely there is a recognition there that is due to people who have managed to re-enter the labour force. I would not be surprised if a few years from now there are amendments to the act to permit the use of unemployment insurance funds
Unemployment Insurance Act for constructing low-cost housing in this country. After all, why not? There are several billions of dollars yearly in the fund. At certain times this substantial source of capital could be used for specific projects.
In essence, Madam Speaker, I have tried to outline this afternoon a series of amendments that we need and which would allow the commission to perform a positive role. I do not subscribe to the theory that the workers abuse the plan. Most Canadians would work if given the chance. This is what they tell us every weekend when we return to our ridings. When we look at what happened in Canada last year and at what happened this year, the pattern that emerges is clearly visible beyond the scope of Bill C-69 which we are now debating. The financial capital is there; it is provided by working Canadians. It amounts to a substantial sum every year. We have the human resources-those people willing to work and who would much rather work than be idle.
The question, then is, when will the political will be there, because surely we can do better than just insure the unemployed or introduce punitive measures some of which are contained in Bill C-69? The system as it is now, as the hon. member for Gloucester (Mr. Breau) said some time ago, can be tightened through better administration. However, the law, the spirit of the unemployment insurance program and the direction that was taken by this parliament in 1971 are sound and require support, particularly in times of high unemployment and difficult economic conditions.

subtopic: UNEMPLOYMENT INSURANCE ACT (1971) MEASURE TO ADD NEW CLASS OF INSURABLE EMPLOYMENT
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I, too, welcome the opportunity to say a few words about Bill C-69 which is a bill to bring forward certain amendments to the Unemployment Insurance Act. I listened with interest to comments by Liberal and Conservative members during this debate, and I was reminded of the description or explanation of what makes a Liberal politician unique, namely, that he is double-jointed and has the ability to sit on the fence and keep his ear to the ground at the same time. The only difference between that and Conservative members is that they are able to stay on both sides of the fence at the same time.
When I listened to criticisms of the bill by certain Liberal members, I wondered how they would vote when this bill came up for third reading. They cannot have their cake and eat it too. If they see, as many of us do in the NDP, that some of these amendments are unfair and will impose undue hardship on the working people, then let them stand up and be counted.
The purpose of the Unemployment Insurance Act is one which I think takes a few minutes to review but is worth reviewing. This act is a response to the problems of unemployment that have plagued Canadian workers for generation after generation. There was the option of leaving it to the soup kitchens and the charitable organizations to provide the destitute unemployed with some means of sustenance, or the belated recognition, mainly due to pressure by the CCF, the forerunner of this party, that in a democratic country the democratically elected government had a certain social obligation to its citizens and a special obligation to the worker who through no fault of his own

November 4, 1975
Unemployment Insurance Act
was thrown on the unemployment rolls. So this act is a social insurance act in that sense. It does provide some minimal income for those who have no other recourse because of the fluctuations of the capitalistic economy in which they work; it does provide financial support for the unemployed worker and his family until he finds new employment.
At the same time, it at least keeps the economy going because it puts purchasing dollars into the hands of the unemployed person so he can buy the necessary consumer goods to keep body and soul together, and in the process keeps manufacturers manufacturing and other workers employed. Let us not forget the necessity and the beneficial aspect of unemployment insurance in that sense. It is not just a hand-out to the individual unemployed person; it is a means of keeping a slowed down economy moving until, hopefully, it comes out of a recession or whatever economic downturn may happen to exist at the time.
Another point that should be remembered is that the unemployment insurance scheme retains for companies and for businessmen a trained working force which has been temporarily laid off. This is a point that is often overlooked. With unemployment insurance those unemployed workers, many of whom are skilled, will continue to reside in the community until there is an upswing; therefore the employer has the benefit of drawing on that pool of skilled labour. If we did not have this program, many of these people would be forced to pull up roots and travel to other parts of the country in the hope of finding a job. So it is a benefit to the employer in that sense as well.
My experience with the local unemployment insurance office in the constituency of Sault Ste. Marie has on the whole been good. I find the staff there quite co-operative. However, the staff is hindered by a multitude of very complicated regulations in the Unemployment Insurance Act. There are times when I feel the unemployed workers are unduly and unfairly victimized because of the complexities of the regulations and the fact that their rights as workers have not been fully explained to them.
I could go through many cases of people who have signed written statements presented to them by UIC officers without fully realizing the implications of signing, and finding to their chagrin at a later time that they had removed the option of appeal and other avenues because they did not fully realize the limitations of the regulations. This is something we cannot legislate; it has to be a policy decision; it has to be a directive from the minister to the local offices to put the regulations and the operation of the act into plain language so the local staffs understand and can interpret them in a plain, forthright manner to the unemployed in order that they are not victimized by the legal jargon and complicated technicalities found in the act.
We have before us today a number of amendments, most of which we in the NDP oppose on the basis that they place an undue financial burden on the unemployed. Our most fundamental objection to this bill is in respect of the change in concept respecting what unemployment insurance is all about. When this plan was set up, there was a built-in incentive for the government to try to reduce unemployment in this country. When the plan was set up, there were to be contributions from employee and employ-

er toward funding the unemployment insurance program. This was to take effect as long as unemployment did not go above 4 per cent of the labour force. If unemployment went above 4 per cent, then the government would supplement the program with money from the consolidated revenue fund. So there was a built-in incentive at that point for the government to keep unemployment down, because if it did not it would have to make up the deficit with tax dollars.
The change we have before us will remove that 4 per cent unemployment ceiling. That move, in itself, is an admission by this Liberal government that unemployment has increased beyond its control and that the government's economic policies have not brought down the unemployment rate in this country but have exacerbated it.
A few years ago the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) was boasting that he would be quite willing to hold tough in his government's battle against inflation by deliberately creating unemployment, and if the rate reached 6 per cent he would be prepared to accept that. Of course, it has gone beyond that now, being in the neighbourhood of 7 per cent, and it might go even higher this winter. So what we have is an admission by this government that its employment policies have failed and that the unemployment situation is worse and will become worse still. I dare say that with this government's wage control policy, people will have less money to spend, there will be less demand and, hence, more unemployment.
The government has now brought in an amendment to let the ceiling on unemployment rise from 4 per cent to 5.8 per cent before it will supplement the plan. That means, quite obviously, that the weekly unemployment insurance premiums for workers and for employers will have to rise accordingly. In effect, by this amendment the government is introducing a regressive tax, not in the sense of an attempt to combat unemployment but a regressive tax only to make up a growing deficit in the fund. Therefore, working people and small businessmen especially will have to pay more from their already diminishing incomes because of the government's inability to control inflation in this country and the government's claim that workers' premiums will rise from the current $1.40 per $100 of earnings to $1.60 or $1.70 per $100 of earnings.
We have made calculations which show that the increase will be around $1.96 for each $100 on income earned because of the projected higher unemployment the country will face this coming winter and the years ahead. Therefore, since the average weekly wage in this country is about $200, the cost of unemployment insurance premiums will not be $2.80 per week, as the government claims, but it will more likely be $3.40 a week, or $176 a year. This is an added expense, an added burden, placed on workers today at the time when the government very cynically brings in a wage control policy that will limit increases in workers' demands to some 10 per cent.
Working Canadians who have seen their wages eroded by inflation escalating at a rate of 11 per cent or 12 per cent over each of the past three years now find their wages controlled by 10 per cent, while at the same time the government slaps a tax on the average worker in respect of the unemployment insurance fund amounting to some $176
November 4, 1975

a year. If that is not regressive and unfair, I do not know what is. We oppose this amendment because of that unfairness and because the government has really given up and does not have any built-in incentive to reduce the unemployment rate.
As unemployment rises, all the government has to do is increase the premiums workers and businessmen have to pay; therefore, the government gets around having to supplement the deficit. In other words, we have the sad state of affairs in which the government has accepted high unemployment as normal. Gone are the days when we were horrified at an unemployment rate of 3 per cent or 4 per cent. Now the government seems to be saying that an unemployment rate of around 5 per cent or 6 per cent is normal and we will have to live with it.
In a country with the resources we have, not only natural but human in terms of skilled workers, that is a sad state of affairs and an admission by this Liberal government that it is bankrupt of ideas with regard to getting the economy stimulated and getting people back to work. Therefore, we will vote against this amendment and oppose it as strongly as we can.
There is another amendment which we find equally reprehensible. I refer to the amendment which would raise the disqualification period for workers who quit their jobs. The plan is to raise the disqualification period from three weeks to six weeks. We must remember, of course, that there is a two-week waiting period in addition. This will mean that the worker who quits his job or is fired will have an eight-week waiting period before he can claim unemployment insurance benefits.
The figures brought forward to justify this change are very interesting. The minister says that the annual rate of those leaving employment is 250,000 workers. I must remind hon. members that this is out of a work force of some 10 million people in this country. That places it in perspective. The annual rate of those who refuse suitable employment out of this work force of 10 million people is only 21,000 workers, or two-tenths of 1 per cent.
Why do people quit their jobs? The reason, I believe, the minister is bringing in this legislation is that he thinks these people are slack, they want to quit, they are not serious about work and want to take advantage of the program. I would like to see statistics to back this up. I am confident the minister could not produce such statistics. When we look at the reasons people leave their employment, we find that in the great majority of cases they have legitimate, valid reasons. For example, the pay may be too low. If an employee has been trying to get a raise over a period of months, and comes up against a stone wall where the employer refuses to give him a raise, and if this employee knows he is worth more than he is receiving, he should have the option to quit and look for another job.
By this amendment, such a person could be frozen into a job classification. This is discriminatory and unfair. It reminds us of the labour practices of the seventeenth century. There could be cases where the employer takes advantage of the worker. We can document many cases where employers have made, shall we say, passes at female employees. That is reprehensible. There are cases involving employers who have demanded that their employees work overtime without pay, or who have demanded that the
Unemployment Insurance Act
employees perform certain jobs which are not classified as part of the regular employment.
Sometimes employers expect employees to perform personal favours for them, and so on. In those circumstances, I would say the employee who quits has a legitimate reason and therefore should have the option of quitting and not being disqualified from unemployment insurance. There are other reasons. Many workers have to quit because of health and working conditions. Near Sault Ste. Marie there is the community of Elliot Lake where the uranimum mines have caused many miners to come down with lung cancer due to silicosis. Would one deny a worker in such circumstances the opportunity to quit his job and receive unemployment insurance benefits?
So, of the 21,000 people who quit and refuse jobs, statistics show that in many cases the reasons are quite legitimate. Therefore, they should not be penalized in the way in which this amendment would penalize them by causing a longer waiting period. I think we should make it very clear that many people who find themselves in the position of having to quit are non-unionized workers. I might remind hon. members that only 33 per cent of the workers in this country belong to labour unions. The unorganized people in the low-paying jobs do not have any kind of bargaining power or back-up to protect their rights. It is they who are victimized by bad working conditions and low pay, and in many cases they have no choice but to quit or be fired if they want to improve their conditions. I must say this amendment is unfair because it discriminates against the unorganized workers in our society.
There is another amendment to the Unemployment Insurance Act with which we also disagree. I cannot for the life of me see how this amendment which is to end the payment of benefits at age 65 will save the government very much money or prevent any kind of real abuse. Currently, unemployment insurance coverage ends at the age of 70 or earlier when a retirement pension becomes payable. What is so unfair about this amendment is, first of all, that those currently between age 65 and age 69 who are working and are insured under the unemployment insurance plan will be automatically cut off from any kind of benefits as a result of this amendment. There is not even the option of a phase-out period for people who in good faith and because of circumstances which have made it impossible for them to retire at 65 have had to stay in the labour force. They will be cut off from benefits in one fell swoop. As I mentioned earlier, those who want to work to the age of 70 at least will no longer have that option once the amendment is passed.
The argument presented by the Liberals for introducing this amendment is that they have taken care of people in their senior years by increasing the old age pension. I must remind them, of course, that that was during the term of a minority government when we forced them to do so. But they say they have increased pensions under the Canada Pension Plan and thus are taking care of people in that age bracket. I would like the minister to try to survive on an old age pension, on some of the Canada Pension Plan payments that retired workers are receiving in my constituency.

Unemployment Insurance Act
I have a horrendous problem in Sault Ste. Marie of zero vacancy rates in apartments. We do not have enough senior citizens' units, and these people are confronted daily with rate increases as well as rising costs of food and medicine. Many of them must continue to work beyond the age of 65. This government will remove that option from them and will remove protection through the Unemployment Insurance Act. I think it is most reprehensible when people who have contributed so much to the growth of our economy through their hard work, and have contributed by paying their premiums into the unemployment insurance scheme, suddenly at the age of 65 find themselves cut off from benefits and are unable to continue working with the security of unemployment insurance protecting them.
I think this government, despite all its claims about how it is interested in and wants to help senior citizens, shows its true spirit, through this amendment, in its attitude toward our older working people. Despite the groans from the Liberal backbenchers, I am sure they know that what I am saying is true because the older people in their constituencies have experienced it.
We also find another example of the niggardliness of this government in these times of high inflation. They have an amendment to reduce the payment to dependants of unemployed workers. Presently, the payments are 75 per cent of insurable earnings for lower paid claimants with dependants. The government is now introducing an amendment which will bring that payment down to 66% per cent for precisely the people who are on low incomes and who are finding it so hard to survive in these days of inflation. On the other hand, if they become unemployed they will be penalized even further by the reduced rate of benefit as a result of this amendment. We say that this is unfair in principle. To try to argue that it will save the government a few dollars does not make sense. One has to take into account the human misery that will be caused to low income people who are unemployed. I agree with my colleagues that this provision should be withdrawn. We will argue that matter in committee.
There are a couple of points in the bill with which my colleagues and I are in agreement. We are not totally negative on the amendments. We are in agreement with the amendment which will extend the qualifying for benefit period. At present, the period in which all claimants may calculate their weeks of insured earnings to qualify for benefit is limited to 52 weeks. Under the proposed change, the qualifying period would be extended to a maximum of 104 weeks for special types of claimants. I am glad the minister has responded to the representations made by opposition members and has recognized that certain people need special consideration; for example, people who are on training courses for 52 weeks and cannot qualify for unemployment insurance premiums because they have not been working in the standard sense of the term in that 52-week period. So we see this move as a progressive step and will support it, as we will the amendments to provide for flexibility in the sickness benefit provisions under the plan.
I do not want to dwell on that matter in detail. Other of my colleagues will do that. I want to reiterate a simple and valid point, namely, that the bulk of the amendments brought forward by the Liberal government will really

force working people to pay for high unemployment caused by the poor and misguided economic policies of this government. This government is giving up the fight on unemployment. It will make the workingman and the businessman in Canada carry the burden of high unemployment by increasing their employment insurance premiums. To add insult to injury, at the time when they are bringing forth these punitive and regressive amendments, this government is bringing in an anti-inflation policy that will control the workers' wages and limit their increases to 10 per cent, in the longer run creating higher unemployment which will reduce consumer spending, causing manufacturing industries to face a slump and lay off workers.
I think this government's legislation to amend the Unemployment Insurance Act is misguided and mistimed. I urge all hon. members to stand up and be counted in committee and on third reading and to vote against these unfortunate and regressive amendments which the minister is proposing in the bill.

subtopic: UNEMPLOYMENT INSURANCE ACT (1971) MEASURE TO ADD NEW CLASS OF INSURABLE EMPLOYMENT
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, in my brief contribution to this interesting debate I want to suggest that one of the more positive and forthright suggestions in the June 23 budget of the former minister of
November 4, 1975

finance was that basic changes would be proposed in the operation of the Unemployment Insurance Commission. The minister pointed out that these changes were necessary for two basic and fundamental reasons: first, UIC costs to the government were becoming unwieldy and, second, the present Unemployment Insurance Act contains, and I quote, "some features which . . . have undesirable effects on work incentives."
Bill C-69, of course, is the instrument of the government to try to face up to our current UIC situation as indicated in the budget of last June. Various amendments are long overdue when we consider that the 1975 UIC pay-out will be approximately $4 billion, while the equivalent pay-out for similar uses in the United States for the year 1973 was about the same dollar figure. That is a most interesting comparison. Further, after three years' experience in my own constituency, the most frequent complaint I receive about UIC is that it is a disincentive to our time-honoured work ethic or, put more bluntly, it is a government institution which very often pays a person not to work.
I wish to begin by making a few comments relating to those three years of personal experience in the Medicine Hat federal constituency. First, however, I should point out that in a letter, the Minister of Manpower and Immigration (Mr. Andras) indicated on August 29, 1975, that we in Medicine Hat had an unemployment rate of only 3.23 per cent, well below the 5 per cent start level for LIP projects, thereby establishing my constituency as eligible only for the minimum allocation of $100,000 for LIP financing. On this very day, by local estimates, my home city of Medicine Hat has some 480 unemployed persons and some 450 available jobs. I suppose it is a situation which could be construed as a negative unemployment rate.
Over these three years of operation of my constituency office, this UIC subject is still the topic brought to my attention most frequently, by a wide margin. The following are a few of the inequities which continue to come to my attention through my constituency office. There is a situation in smaller rural towns which precludes a worker from becoming eligible for benefits unless he moves to a different area to continue his job search routine. There is another situation where a husband is moved to a smaller area; his wife gives up her job to move with him and then runs into trouble establishing eligibility for benefits when she gives up that job.
The requirement of 20 insured weeks to qualify for sickness or pregnancy benefits can involve hardships which bear no relation to regular claims, which require only eight insured weeks with a much longer benefit period possible. There is an instance of a woman having a heart attack after 18 weeks and being unable to qualify for UIC benefits because she did not have the required 20 weeks of insured work. Again, in the case of sickness benefits, the regulation calling for a two-week waiting period after application is not clearly understood by many of those who apply, neither is the implication of a sickness claim which is only valid over the initial 15 weeks.
Overpayments are a continuing and often embarrassing source of annoyance. Surely some procedural improvement is possible here instead of the lame excuse of computer
Unemployment Insurance Act
errors. These tempting overpayments invite illegal action by younger recipients and cause extreme frustration and annoyance to elderly people. The job search routine, especially during winter months, seems to present special frustrations to elderly workers which lead to misunderstanding and sometimes hardship.
I mention these specific experiences from my constituency office in order more fully to support the statement that in my opinion almost every UIC problem brought to my attention is a personal and private one to which it is difficult to apply the UIC regulations and difficult to categorize. It seems to me that some form of means test could be instituted to respond more completely to these personal and private situations to which I have referred. I do not suggest that this means test be applied to all UIC claims, only that it be an optional procedure which could very well be of great assistance to the board of referees.
I shall now make some brief comments on the bill itself. I fully support the proposal to increase the disqualification period from three to six weeks for those who quit, are fired or refuse suitable employment. I have heard some representations that this disqualification period should be extended even more. The decision of the government to raise the break-even benchmark for self-financing from 4 per cent unemployment to a moving eight-year unemployment average is a clear indication to me that this government has given up on our persistent and seemingly ever-increasing unemployment problem. It is an inward-looking, passive and unimaginative attitude which surely is not acceptable.
While it is true that the increased premiums to be shared by employers and employees, plus the added costs due to this increased benchmark for self-financing, will amount to a considerable saving to the government, it is really an added cost or tax of considerable magnitude to all employers and employees. The cost is still there, and as the press has already pointed out, this change in UIC financing could reach an additional total for 1976 from $800 million to $1 billion, more than double the recent ten-cent gasoline excise tax total.

subtopic: UNEMPLOYMENT INSURANCE ACT (1971) MEASURE TO ADD NEW CLASS OF INSURABLE EMPLOYMENT
speechtext:
In many cases it did help. I listened to the hon. member for Timmins (Mr. Roy) who raised the question of abuses. This has been referred to by other speakers. One point he did raise referred to clause 11 and the claiming procedure for sickness benefits which can be undertaken during the first 25 weeks on claim rather than the first 15 weeks. That is a step in the right direction. Unfortunately, I cannot say the same thing about all the proposed amendments.
The hon. member for St. Catharines (Mr. Parent) raised a very good point. There is a popular misconception in this country that people like to go on unemployment insurance for 52 weeks, but the hon. member pointed out that the average for an individual on benefits is 16 weeks. He also said that the amendment referring to those people over 65 years of age would be understood by them. I do not think it will, Madam Speaker.
The hon. member for Halton (Mr. Philbrook) also referred to abuses. He said this amendment would reduce the payments by the government. That is true; it loads them right on to the workingman and the businessman. He also referred to the amendment correcting abuses and said it rationalizes the plan. That is a vague statement. It rationalizes the plan to the extent that it unloads responsibility from the government on to workingmen and women.
Yesterday, the hon. member for Spadina (Mr. Stollery) said he had heard nothing but contradictions from the opposition. I suppose in a democratic parliament one is liable to hear these opinions. There is one other matter I would like to mention, the question of having to indicate to the Unemployment Insurance Commission that you have searched for a job in four or five places. As far as I am concerned the official employment agency in Canada is Canada Manpower. It is supposed to have its finger on the pulse of industry, knowing every place that workers may be needed. If they cannot find employment how can they expect an individual to find it?
An individual must apply for work at four or five different places. If there are no jobs available he must ask for a letter saying that he has applied. In an area like mine it is absolutely ridiculous. You can wear out your feet looking for a job. You just cannot find one. Before leaving the comments of different members I want to say that I agree with much of what was said by the hon. member for Regina-Lake Centre. It was the inflated member for Hamilton Mountain who made the interjection. It is a pretty sad commentary on those 65 and over who have contributed to this country for a lifetime. Many of those over 65 are still working. They certainly should not be referred to as work dodgers. That is a bit serious to make that kind of remark.
Bill C-69 is nothing more than a government rip off against the people of this nation to whom the government pledged it would give the greatest possible protection. It more and more produces evidence that Liberal times are hard times. The workers of this nation will pay the bill for the government's almost unbelievable incompetence and ineptitude in managing the economy of the country.
The government created unemployment just a few short years ago. It said that that was the answer. We were told that by creating unemployment it would remedy the economy of the country. It got on a downhill slide. It is now having to take more and more money from the working men and women of this country to pay for the problem it has created.
We have moved from an unemployment insurance scheme that was actuarially sound and only in trouble in times of deep recession to one that has become an added tax on most of the work force and most businesses. While the workingman and the businessman have to pay the bill they have little to say about the size of that bill. Most derive absolutely no benefit from the tax they pay.
Since 1968 the government with its Trudeaucrats has completely obliterated the image meticulously developed that Liberals, and only Liberals, are the competent managers of the economy. They like to blast the Diefenbaker administration every chance they get. However, those who examine the performance of that administration yearn for that administration that year after year produced a rate of inflation of less than 1 per cent. What is the rate of inflation at this time? The Diefenbaker administration scored triumph after triumph in developing our increased gross national product, while at the same time finding jobs for the many thousands who entered the work force. Since this minister is also in charge of immigration, he will remember the situation in Europe in 1956 when several hundred thousand hit the labour market of this country.
The government goes to any length to transfer its major miscalculations to others. No group of Canadians, including the poor and the aged, are exempt from its mad dash to eliminate the responsibility for its mistakes.
It is hard to believe that Bill C-69 clearly sets out that those 65 years of age and over will not receive benefits under the amended UIC legislation. It clearly discriminates against them. What an achievement, laying it on the backs of the older people of this country.
Approximately 5,000 Canadians will either be forced out of the work force or find it difficult to continue working. This is being done for a miserly saving of $3 million. The taxpayers' contribution to bolster the fund to meet the demand of claimants runs from $1,750 million to $2 billion, depending on how high the rate of inflation goes.
This legislation says to the working men and women who have trouble keeping pace with skyrocketing inflation that it will be made more severe, or that their pay cheques will be that much thinner as a result of this added tax or

November 4, 1975
Unemployment Insurance Act
higher contribution. They are also told that inflation will be promoted by higher costs for the products they will purchase in the market place. The businessman will have to go to the same market place to recover the same payments he must make to the fund. And those sums are not to be sneezed at-they are expected to be in the area of $800 million to $1 billion next year, amounting to an average extra tax on every person paying into the fund equal to some $89 yearly.

speechtext: Completely inaccurate.

subtopic: UNEMPLOYMENT INSURANCE ACT (1971) MEASURE TO ADD NEW CLASS OF INSURABLE EMPLOYMENT
speechtext:
Well, the minister will have his opportunity to speak when he takes part in the debate later on. If the unemployment bench mark moves from the present 4 per cent to 5.3 per cent, it is expected the breakdown will be something like $443 million from employers and $317 million from workers; it could well be more if the unemployment rate jumps above the present 7.2 per cent to 8 per cent or higher.
Also, it is nothing short of rank discrimination against the worker to tell him he will face a six weeks disqualification if he quits his job. That amounts to a month and a half plus the two-week waiting period, after which he has to face the delays and the letters couched in legalese, involved language, and bureacratic jargon. That is one of the points I should like to comment on. For Heaven's sake let them get down to using normal language in these letters they send out to claimants instead of language which even lawyers sometimes fail to understand.
The minister would be doing a good service to the working people of Canada if he would instruct his staff to get down to earth and put the statements contained in their letters and documents into language people can understand. However, I was talking about the delay occasioned by long delays in payments. Not many workers can accept an attack on their limited savings for six or eight weeks.
Then again there can be many reasons for leaving employment. I appreciate, of course, that there should be investigations associated with such cases, but I believe each case should be treated individually and action taken on individual cases as warranted. The amendment put forward smacks of total discrimination against the worker and places a valuable weapon in the hand of the employer. Some hon. members may ask why. Well, I still have my little card from the National Employment Service; I am not as old as the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles), but I do have the card. I was among the lucky ones; fortunately, I never had to draw unemployment insurance benefits, unlike millions of other Canadians.
When investigations and so on are in progress, a weapon is immediately put into the hands of employers. I have run into a number of employers across the country who have said to people in their work force, "Either do this, or that, or you are not with us any more". The task indicated might be altogether apart from the work the man is supposed to do. As I say, there can be many reasons which compel a man to leave his job. This is an area which should be carefully analyzed and each case should be judged on its merits.

I wish to say a few words now about abuses. It is a favourite topic. Like every other member of the House I do not condone abuses of the unemployment insurance fund and I favour every step being taken to eliminate the blood suckers. I state definitely that I will support every effort by the minister to prevent abuses of the fund, because the more abuses there are the harder it is for those with legitimate claims to get their claims recognized. Abuse creates suspicion in the minds of those who work within the Unemployment Insurance Commission. They are apt to approach claims with the attitude that the claimant is probably just another character trying to get money which is not really due to him. As a result the applicant with a legitimate case is screened carefully, and settlement of his claim is likely to be delayed as well.
Sometimes we can overdo this concern about abuses. As the hon. member for St. Catharines said, everyone seems to think that once a worker's claim to benefit is allowed he remains in receipt of benefit for 50 weeks or 52 weeks. That is not correct. The average period is 16 weeks. And often, because of some bureaucratic difficulty about which an innocent claimant is not aware, payments come to an end.
I represent an area which, unfortunately, has consistently returned an unemployment rate running two or three times the national average. Unemployment insurance benefits are absolutely essential in order to maintain the work force during periods of trouble which never seem to cease to plague the area. We also have a great many older citizens within the work force, and because of the continuing high rate of unemployment and the inability of workers to move from one job to another-simply because the opportunities are not there, unlike the situation in other parts of the nation-the legislation before us is bound to discriminate against older members of the work force and place employers in a position to threaten the work force with the weapon of six weeks' disqualification.
Yesterday the hon. member for Cumberland-Colchester North (Mr. Coates) made a suggestion which I believe to be worthy of consideration. In the course of his remarks he said:
We should have a scheme whereby those who work and never draw benefits but pay into the fund day after day, year in and year out, would be able to receive some benefit in a realistic way at the end of their working careers. If they work continually and contribute to the fund they should derive some benefit for the contributions they have made over a lifetime.
I am not an actuarial expert; in fact I am not an expert in anything, but I think something along these lines could be worked out and I commend the suggestion to the minister. There are many millions of people who contribute to the fund week after week and year after year without drawing benefit, and possibly a certain proportion of the fund could be set aside for such a purpose as my hon. friend proposed. At the end of their working lives they would receive a payment in some form, taking into consideration the size of the amount which had been taken from the fund. The amount would be based on the record. Such a scheme might discourage people from drawing a benefit needlessly; they might well look ahead and say. "The time may come when I shall need some extra help when I choose to retire."

Let us consider some of the reaction to this bill. This is from the Gazette of June 28, 1975, and the writer is Don McGillivray, a financial analyst:
The change in unemployent insurance financing faces Canadian employees and employers with an additional tax burden at least twice as heavy as the extra tax on gasoline . . . this extra payroll tax under the new formula may reach $800 million to $1 billion next year. The new tax load will amount to an average of $89 or more a year on the wages and salaries of all Canadians who work for a pay check.
Then there are the comments of Joe Morris, President of the C.L.C., in a press release on July 21. He said of the proposal that:
Low income workers chiefly will bear the burden of longer penalty periods, elimination of benefit for workers age 65 and other money saving provisions ... It appears that the government seeks to slowly but surely reduce the social security protection now afforded Canadians by the social legislation it has taken the trade union movement and kindred groups so many years to establish.

speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I am pleased to take part in this debate on Bill C-69, an Act to amend the Unemployment Insurance Act, 1971. This amending legislation introduces a new class of insurable employment.
Any member that will listen to his constituents will know that unemployment, or at least the lack of steady revenue, is a continuing concern and a day-to-day problem with thousands of Canadians.
Unemployment figures published monthly by Statistics Canada make the headlines each time there is an increase. Surveys show unemployment is always the most urgent and dramatic problem in the people's mind.
Amendments made by the government to the Unemployment Insurance Act, either to add to or delete from classes of claimants are but useless patchwork, not to say harmful patchwork. The way the government amends the act, it would appear that by changing drivers it believes its jalopy will become a Cadillac. The engine is worn out, all four tires are flat, the suspension is finished, the transmission whines, but the government seems to think that by changing drivers, everything will be better.
Bill C-69 is the latest of a series. The government realizes the unemployment insurance program is inadequate, but rather than bringing the scheme on a sounder and more logical foundation, it introduces minor amendments that do nothing to meet the real needs and expectations of Canadians.
Before discussing one by one the amendments proposed in Bill C-69, it is essential in my view to note that the minister and the government as a whole do not understand the meaning and the nature of the unemployment problem now facing Canada. This lack of understanding of the actual causes of unemployment explains why this government is bringing in such a ridiculous legislation as Bill C-69.
Unemployment Insurance Act
The first distinction the government seems unable to make is the one between "unemployed" and "without income". The government has always made known its wish to achieve full employment. Not so long ago, the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) made quite a radical statement saying that if the government had the power to do what it pleases, it could put an end to unemployment by compelling workers to go where jobs are available.
If you apply this principle a little further, you end up with hard labour camps in the Arctic, which would not fail to please the Prime Minister who expressed all his admiration during his trip to Soviet Union for developments in Siberia.
We know that the work there has been done by millions of people sentenced to hard labour by the Moscow dictatorship. The basic principle guiding the government in the face of unemployment is to seek full employment. A job for everyone is the priority of this government. However, the real unemployment problem, the real tragedy of millions of unemployed Canadians is not to be without a job, but to be without a regular income.
Let us consider the unemployed. What is their problem? They do not have any money. They cannot buy the bread and butter needed to feed their family. They cannot buy the clothing and all the items required to keep their family warm and secure. It is always a matter of money. Even this government which would have us believe that the individual problem of unemployment can be solved through full employment. It is recognized that the real problem of the unemployed is primarily one of income. In fact, when it came to taking action against unemployment, the government established unemployment insurance benefits to provide an income to those without any.
It is then obvious that what is considered as an unemployment insurance problem is actually an income problem. Even if the government made a step forward by recognizing, maybe unknowingly, that the jobless must have an income, the efforts in this field are still based on the false principle that full employment or the fact of giving a job to everyone is the final solution to the unemployment problem.
Brought to its logical conclusion, that principle would disregard all technical progress which resulted in the elimination of some occupations. Power shovels would be replaced by labourers with pick and shovel. Farm tractors would be replaced by horses. Finally, a man will be substituted for a horse since it would take a job from another man.
With this foolish rule, we will soon return to the prehistoric age when a man did everything manually. This is the conclusion, Madam Speaker, to which leads full employment. A machine can do in ten minutes the work and production of 1,000 men. Now, Madam Speaker, what remains to be done? Destroy that machine and make a man work very hard. Madam Speaker, may I say that it is six o'clock?

subtopic: UNEMPLOYMENT INSURANCE ACT (1971) MEASURE TO ADD NEW CLASS OF INSURABLE EMPLOYMENT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, as I was saying just before recess at six o'clock: Is it logical? Is it clever? And yet, it stems from the principle of full employment. For years, the Social Credit Party has been advocating a guaranteed minimum income. The important thing, is to put into the hands of the people an income that will enable them to buy the products available in Canada. When 1,000 workers are laid-off because technology and progress dictate that they should be replaced by one machine that will do their work ten times faster, what are we to do? Destroy the machine on account of the absurd principle of full employment, because it deprives 1,000 men of their work, or distribute to these workers replaced by the machine the income derived from the use of a more efficient and more profitable means of production?
Because the government advocates full employment rather than efficiency and productivity, thousands of Canadians are kept in useless jobs. Instead of giving them their share of the machine-made production, machines are scrapped and men put to work needlessly. An unemployment rate of 7 to 8 per cent means that the entire production can be made available 92 per cent of the available manpower.
Dr. Richard Belman, an American specialist of production methods stated that the entire present production could be obtained with 2 per cent of the present manpower. In other words, the products we now have could be available with a 98 per cent rate of unemployment. This could be made possible if the government was not fighting technological progress and advances.
Of course, Mr. Speaker, the problem to be solved is how to distribute to all those removed from the production process an income that will allow them to benefit from the abundance of products available to them thanks to automation. That is the challenge we have to meet now in Canada. The government should stop listening to such stupid economists who say: Better employ people at digging ditches they will fill afterwards, than not employing them at all.
Mr. Speaker, the government should rather listen to the solutions proposed by Social Crediters and free Canadians from the tasks machines can do in their place. In a coherent system, the machine must be at the service of man, not man at the service of the machine. To the extent that they make it possible to distribute to the unemployed an income which enables them to buy the many products available, unemployment insurance benefits are acceptable and desirable. Unfortunately, the Unemployment Insurance Act, like the amendments discussed today for that matter, is too often only a means of placing workers in the power of the government and civil servants. Mr. Speaker, in 1973, no fewer than 92,871 Canadians were disqualified from unemployment insurance benefits under Unemployment Insurance Act regulation 145 alone, because an almighty civil servant considered that they had not sought employment actively enough.
[The Acting Speaker (Mrs. Morin).]
In 1974 the number of disentitlements was over 93,000. This is only one example and we could give many more. Thus, the provision of Bill C-69 now under study which will double the penalty for an individual who voluntarily quits his job is just another measure which does not consider the particular situation of each individual. And what shall we say about the fact that Bill C-69 takes away from people aged 65 their rights to benefits? It is an unacceptable measure and I would be tempted to support the hon. member who suggested to the Minister of Manpower and Immigration (Mr. Andras) who had proved his openmindedness by proposing at least five amendments aiming at significantly improving the Unemployment Insurance Act, that he should consider the possibility of giving workers aged 65 or over the opportunity to express their desire to withdraw from the unemployment insurance plan, to receive the three weeks' benefits provided for in the government's bill and to allow all those who wish to continue working to pay premiums, which means accepting all responsibilities and obligations stemming from the plan.
That being said, Mr. Speaker, I think it would be logical for the minister to move this amendment to the legislation. The government has no right to say to people of 65 or over: "Go away from the labour market, we have no more room for you." The UIC cases submitted to us by our constituents can be counted by the hundreds within a month. The root cause of the problem is an administrative decision or the interpretation of a nebulous regulation by officials who suffer from delusions of grandeur. Sometimes, Mr. Speaker, one has to go all the way up to the department to get justice and have the mistakes corrected.
By the way, I would like to thank the minister for the cases I submitted to him and which have been settled to the advantage of the claimants. Last May 5 I submitted to the minister five cases which the Unemployment Insurance Commission office of my riding could not settle and the minister really proved to be very helpful to us. But I have to point out that a more logical and realistic system would probably put an end to all those problems which are extremely annoying for the members of the four parties in the House.
That is why I believe that the government should listen to the suggestions made by Socred members and should consider a thorough reform not only of the unemployment insurance plan but also of the whole economic system. If the government, instead of trying to achieve full employment by eliminating the abundance that would result from a greater productivity thanks to an improved technology, would give to the people the financial means and the purchasing power required to buy the available production, the problem of unemployment insurance would be completely solved. With the machine, people would gradually free themselves of manual jobs and they could develop more and more and improve the country through creative and rewarding activities. Some people believe that a system based on the distribution of a national dividend to all individuals depending on the available production would be a disincentive to work.
As the Social Credit leader said: Show me only one lazy millionnaire. It means that the individual who has the
November 4, 1975

income he needs will automatically be hard working instead of being lazy. Social Credit would not discourage private enterprise as does the present system. Unlike the present system, Social Credit would not compel the individual who draws benefits to stay at home and decline work offers. In a Social Credit system, the individual would receive his national dividend and would be encouraged to add this amount to his salary.
Social Credit proposes a modern system taking into account technical progress and human nature. The individual benefits from technical progress through national dividends and is encouraged to add this amount to anything he can earn through personal initiative. And being paid to everyone this dividend will be fair to all Canadians. That is the Social Credit alternative!
I ask this government now that we are studying Bill C-69 concerning unemployment insurance to review its position and the basic principles upon which its obsolete unemployment insurance system lays. I am sure it is also the wish of all Canadians who believe in the future of their country.
