speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I think it is quite interesting to take part in this debate, not to advocate revolutionary solutions, nor to attack an opposition far more bent on criticizing the bill than finding out advantages for the population, but simply, Mr. Speaker, to remind hon. members that the philosophy underlying unemployment insurance is sometimes misunterstood. Unfortunately, in too many circles that legislation is misinterpreted. I am not contending that opposition members are the only ones responsible for those misinterpretations, and I, as a government member, take my share of the blame for the view, prevalent among the public, that unemployment insurance is a form of social assistance.
Mr. Speaker, I think it is time for politicians to assume a minimum of responsibilities and tell people frankly why we introduced and passed that act. To some people, especially claimants, it is too stringent a legislation. Those who draw unemployment insurance benefits claim, sometimes rightly, that the waiting period before they can be paid benefits is too long.
Several mentioned it, my friends in the opposition pointed it out, and sometimes rightly so. It is normal that the person who applies to the UIC should not have to wait too long before getting the money he needs most of the time to secure his right to live. And I deplore that on many occasions the system set up does not achieve the normal objectives that the people have a right to expect. I wonder, Mr. Speaker, whether behind that bureacracy, those electronic machines probably designed to improve the legislation, did not accomplish exactly the opposite in certain quarters.

subtopic: UNEMPLOYMENT INSURANCE ACT (1971) MEASURE TO ADD NEW CLASS OF INSURABLE EMPLOYMENT
speechtext: That is also true.

subtopic: UNEMPLOYMENT INSURANCE ACT (1971) MEASURE TO ADD NEW CLASS OF INSURABLE EMPLOYMENT
speechtext:
I think we should gradually come back to a more human approach towards the claimant who, after all, finds himself in an extremely difficult situation, through his fault or not, whether he quit his job voluntarily or was laid off because no job was available for him. Mr. Speaker, I think it is important to try and find within our
Unemployment Insurance Act
system, which theoretically is excellent, some means to improve it and make it more effective. May I be allowed to make a suggestion to hon. members. I had the opportunity this afternoon to discuss with the manager of my local UIC office. He told me that they made an experiment in our area. They sent to 100 persons chosen at random notices informing them that they would no longer be getting their unemployment insurance benefits, without giving them the reason for that decision. Out of the 100 persons who received that notice only 50 answered and objected and asked for an explanation. Then they were simply told, very well, you can have your unemployment insurance back.
This seems to show that the mail delivery system for cheques seems to be used by several claimants to receive benefits that do not belong to them. I come to the conclusion, and the manager agrees with me, that it would be a good thing to revert to the system under which the claimant must come and collect his cheque. Of course, this requires a measure of decentralization, opening offices closer to the people so that they would not have to cover long distances to collect their cheques. But I think this would make the act more effective and ensure that those who come to collect their cheques are entitled to them. And I make that suggestion in a constructive way. I do not want to find fault with the public in general nor with the claimants, but it seems to me that here we have a problem which could be solved by reaching two objectives: making the law more humane and perhaps avoiding greater expenses, since this is one of the goals we are aiming at with the legislation we brought in and with the amendments we are putting before the House.
Mr. Speaker, I was saying that the unemployment insurance concept, as people understand it, was warped in certain quarters.
Mr. Speaker, I think I should recall that unemployment insurance is an insurance, as the name says. It is temporary insurance made available to those who are on the labour market but cannot immediately find employment.
I think I was repeating what every hon. member could say when I said that some people come to us and insist that they paid unemployment insurance for months and for years and that they have a right to get benefits as long as provided by the act. Mr. Speaker, I think it is time we emphasize in no uncertain terms that unemployment insurance is a right of recipients, but in given circumstances.
The first condition to be met by the claimant is what my friend opposite, the hon. member for Villeneuve (Mr. Caouette) did not seem to take into account when he spoke about people who had been excluded because they did not take the necessary steps. Mr. Speaker, it is elementary!
A few months or a few years ago, you only had to stop working, stay home, complete a form and wait for your cheque for a certain number of weeks, most often, the maximum number provided, as though it was due to you.
Mr. Speaker, I believe it is absolutely essential and moreover normal to ask the claimant not only to register with the manpower office, but also to look for a job.
Obviously, people must exercise some judgment and common sense in looking for a job. It is impossible to ask the claimant to go personally to prospective employers dozens of times every week, but he must make an effort, he

November 4, 1975
Unemployment Insurance Act
is not required to find a job, but only to cooperate in looking for work and to show, by his availability and his efforts, that he is interested in finding a job.
Mr. Speaker, I would like to touch on an extremely sensitive aspect of this legislation, a point about which many members have expressed their views. I believe that it is my duty to try to explain my opinion about the provision which, if passed, would prevent people aged 65 from receiving unemployment insurance benefits.
Mr. Speaker, I believe that those who say that we do not respect people who are retired distort the meaning of this legislation. It is precisely because we have consideration and respect for people who are 65 that we are passing this legislation.
Mr. Speaker, we believe that a 65 year old citizen who has worked for society deserves to be no longer in the obligation of working hard to earn his living and support himself and his family. We believe that he has reached an age where he deserves certain benefits from society which will allow him to live comfortably without having to earn a living.
I think, Mr. Speaker, that it is normal to say to an individual who has reached age 65: "You can obtain the old age security pension, the supplement as well as your superannuation fund or an annuity. You can even work if you wish." There is every kind of opportunity and assistance for people who are 65 years old.
Mr. Speaker, I do not suggest that those measures are perfect, that they are sufficient and enable the 65 year-olds to live in wealth and affluence. No, I do not say so. But I feel there are some who play politics by saying to those people: "Through that legislation the government wants to harm you and does not understand your problems." That is not responsible nor honest. I think it is essential to say to those people: "The Unemployment Insurance Act is a legislation meant to protect the worker." It is designed for the worker just as the old age security pension is not paid to those who are 45, 50 or 62; we pay it to people of 65. It would be abnormal to give people of 65 years and over the same benefits available to those under 65. In fact, Mr. Speaker, I am sure that the people over 65 would understand this bill if someone explained it to them frankly and made it clear to them that it is intended to do away with the confusion which exists in this act at the present time and to help those who are now on the labour market and are temporarily unable to find a job. It may happen that a person will pay premiums all his or her life without ever collecting unemployment insurance benefits, but he or she should rejoice for having had the courage, the luck and the good fortune of working and earning a living without living off the State.
With this in mind, Mr. Speaker, I feel it is possible in all fairness and honesty to understand that the purpose of this bill is to put unemployment insurance back in its true perspective. I even wonder at times if we did not go a little too far in this legislation by trying to accommodate, to please everyone, to the extent where it has lost its real purpose, that of helping those who are temporarily out of work. I say it again, we do not aim at depriving other needy citizens of what other forms of assistance may be at

their disposal. But the fact remains, and I am convinced of this, Mr. Speaker, that the amendments proposed, in addition to achieving real savings, tie in with the objectives the act should achieve, to make it easier for those who are entitled to benefits to get them while preventing those who try to take undue advantage of the act from doing so through appropriate penalties.
To my mind, Mr. Speaker, this bill does not meet with the approval of all categories of citizens since it affects some of them.
This legislation is the expression of a minister's feelings in an attempt to put some order in a measure that had gone beyond its objectives and had lost a little of its orientation. We are returning to a legislation that seems to me more just, more honest.
I hope hon. members will understand that since I represent a working class, I am in a position to understand the meaning of the statement I am making this evening, the importance it can have among my constituents. But I believe I am honest enough to express it very sincerely so that they will know that if I accept to vote in favour of this measure it is because I believe it will help the worker, because he is the one who pays for it, he is the one who has the right to request the government to find ways to reduce unemployment insurance costs. Often the worker says: the laws enacted by the government are not helping us. I feel this is a law that will help the worker. Clearly, there will be an extra cost but the savings made thanks to the proposed amendments may show we are going in the right direction.
To conclude, I would urge those of my constituents that might read these remarks to cooperate with us in trying to find those who rip off the program. Too often, people call our constituency offices and state they know of people receiving benefits unduly. But when asked for names, they will not say because "they wish no harm to anybody". I hope people will understand that in so doing, they would help us fulfill the true goals of the act.
People must help us, they must try and understand that we want to go in the right direction. If it turned out that the bill did not meet its aims, if it were more harm than good, I would be the first to say so. Because I belong to a party in which I am not forced to blindly accept any proposals, a party that allows me to discuss matters. We may make mistakes, but I do not believe we are making one now. We are going to pass the bill, and if it does not really help those we wish to help, I believe we should and will bring in further amendments.
For this reason, I fully support the bill. I hope that, if it does not bring the expected results, the government will introduce other amendments to make the act more efficient, more honest and more helpful to the unemployed.

subtopic: UNEMPLOYMENT INSURANCE ACT (1971) MEASURE TO ADD NEW CLASS OF INSURABLE EMPLOYMENT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I welcome this opportunity to enter into the debate on this bill with regard to unemployment insurance because of the involvement I have had over the past three years with the people in my riding who wonder just what is going on in the field of unemployment insurance. We need only look at the record to see that something is certainly wrong and has been wrong because the cost of our unem-
November 4, 1975

ployment insurance scheme in Canada is now up to approximately $4 billion, which is up from $1.8 billion in 1972, or an increase of 186 per cent in the past three years.
In 1972 unemployment insurance made up 1.51 per cent of the gross national product. In 1975 we see it as 2.72 per cent of the gross national product, and when we consider that Canada, with just over 20 million people, has a cost of unemployment insurance the same as the United States with over 200 million people we begin to wonder what really is taking place.
We read in the Vancouver Province of June 19, 1975, headlines indicating that Ottawa will not compel workers to take jobs. We read that the Minister of Manpower and Immigration (Mr. Andras) told the Senate Committee examining federal manpower policy that the government will not force workers to accept jobs they do not want. In a riding such as mine this sort of thing makes people very uptight, especially when they know about UIC ski teams and when they see young people walking around the cities or on the beach having a good time in the sun. They know there is 20 per cent unemployment in the Okanagan Valley, and that the mines and the lumber mills in the area cannot get enough people to work. No wonder a statement such as this makes them uptight and they write to their member of parliament.
We also hear of many abuses of the unemployment insurance scheme, and I get many complaints from my constituents. Maybe not all are legitimate but some of them are, and people are very concerned.
I think we must decide whether this should be a welfare scheme or an insurance scheme, Mr. Speaker. I submit it is really a welfare scheme. It has taught people not to work and, as a result, we are losing the work ethic in Canada.
I know that the unemployment insurance offices have people in the field trying to police the scheme, but in most cases it is the innocent who get caught. Some people have worked 20 or 30 years, have paid into the scheme, and for some reason find themselves unemployed. Then they have to fall back on unemployment insurance. These people are not experienced in beating the system and we know that those who are experienced in this sort of thing are hard to catch. The easy ones are caught and an example is made of them. Usually they are quite innocent people who do not know how to manipulate the system.
At the moment there is a post office strike and some unemployment insurance offices are open on Saturdays so that people can get their cheques. In my riding the first day they were open 45 per cent of the people did not pick up their cheques. We do not even know if they are still in the country. Why should they not pick up their cheques? This seems to suggest that a lot of people are abusing the system. They might not even be in the area or could be out working-they could even have two or three different names on the list.
The strike has taught us that we should stop mailing these cheques. People should go to the office to pick up their payment. After all, they are unemployed and should have more time than anybody else. They should be available when the payment is ready.
Unemployment Insurance Act
The Manpower offices and unemployment insurance offices should be put together, with an emphasis on Manpower. Shortly after I was elected I went into the new federal building in Kelowna to visit the Manpower office and the unemployment insurance office. The latter was on the second floor and very easy to get at, but the Manpower office was on the third floor and down a hall at the back end of the building. I think the reverse should be the rule, with the Manpower office easy to find, not the unemployment insurance office.
I should like to read a letter from one of my constituents which originally appeared in the Penticton Herald. I think it points out what I am talking about. It is headed "A Mother Pleads For Help", and reads as follows:
In a cheek out line at a local grocery store today, I was behind five husky, beautifully tanned young men who made their food purchases with food vouchers. They reminded me of construction workers with their big brown bodies-or beach bums-and I here confess, without facts, I suspected the latter. Later I watched them drive away in a late 1960 auto.
I watched too, the faces of the young female clerk and even younger packer as they put the groceries in bags and did the necessary signing of forms. When my turn came, I commented that it was unbelievable that five healthy males would need food vouchers with local orchardists begging for pickers . (My own 15 and 12 year olds are picking cherries part of a day). The clerk said it really "gets you down" when you see as many as ten some days going through her checkout alone.
So when I got home, I phoned Human Resources and asked how this was possible. The gentleman told me transients are given food vouchers of $5 only when they have proof that are going to a job. (In my cynical manner I wondered how they check up on that!!) I told the chap I was annoyed. No one minds widows and orphans, but adult healthy males are another thing. I told him of the faces and feelings of the working folk I had observed, and became more annoyed as I talked.
He finally said, "How would you feel if you had a job to go to and no money for food?" Now how, thought I, can he possibly know the total facts about a person, after an hour's interview-even days of interviewing? I am not the only one who thinks emotionally and irrationally, without knowing all the facts at times. So do trained social workers and governments who propose and pass legislation on an emotional basis.
My answer to him was fact, I believe. These young men knew yesterday that they would have to eat today. They were intelligent (to take advantage of a system) and educated; they spoke and wrote and drove a car.
And that reminded me of our recent holiday and a notice we read while deep in the Oregon mountains, where the beautiful cheeky Stellar's blue jays ate right out of our hands. It said, "Please do not feed the wild life. By doing so, you attract unusually large numbers to the area, which in turn over use and destroy their environment. The animals gradually forget to forage for themselves. The squirrels and chipmunks forget to store food. When the winter comes, they will destroy themselves. In other words, your charity can kill them."
We are not so concerned with our environment, yet here we go, disturbing and destroying our human ecology. For the saddest thing about this whole story is not what we have given to those young men, but what we are taking away from them. We have taken away their ability to face a problem and think their own way out of a dilemma. We are conditioning young people to a reliance on the state to solve problems, and this is an erosion of the individual's independence and responsibility. Again we have taken away pride and self respect, proof of which is the acceptance of charity while able to work.
But the greatest thing we have taken away from them is their "spirit," the life blood of any nation. And so sadly, and by and far, more dangerous, this same "spirit" is what I watched, fading from the faces and speech of the young clerks in the grocery store, by a system which no longer rewards healthy minds and bodies at work, but instead taxes them to death, both physically and mentally. Yes, it does "get you down." No wonder there is a tremendous increase in artificially "blotted spirits" and prescribed, or otherwise, drugs.

November 4, 1975
Unemployment Insurance Act
This epistle must cease. My 12 year old has just come bounding through the door, proudly announcing he earned $5 picking cherries today. Please society-you and I-let's not kill his spirit with irrational kindness.
This lady has put it very well. I might say that a tremendous number of copies of this letter to the editor were sent to me. It sets out very well what is happening in my constituency.
Unemployment insurance should be a program that helps people when going from one job to another. It should be an insurance scheme. Other members of my party have ably pointed out the salient points of this bill. Those aged 65 will no longer receive benefits. I do not know how the government rationalizes that when all that will be saved will be approximately $3 million.
I received a telephone call today from one of my constituents who is approaching the age of 65. He has paid into the unemployment insurance plan all his life. Now that he is about to retire, he will not receive any benefit. He will not receive the full Canada Pension Plan benefits because he has not been on the plan long enough. He has paid into the unemployment insurance plan and feels he should receive some benefit. Under the regulations he must be looking for a job in order to enjoy the benefits.
I had to agree with this person that there are many people who receive unemployment insurance most of the time. They only have to work for two months to receive the benefits. Even though they have to wait eight weeks, that is not much of a hardship for many of those who do not want to work. If they know how to manipulate the system they can go for a year or even better without working. They do what they know best, and that is what we are teaching them, namely, to watch work. I often say that I like work so well that I can sit and watch it all day. This man knows what is going on. He feels that be is being discriminated against. I have to agree with him as the amount that will be saved is low.
The low income worker is the one who will be hurt. The cost of it is being put on to the backs of the poor. It is not designed to save a great amount of money, to get people used to the work ethic again, or find jobs for those who are unemployed.
I do not wish to delay this debate. However, I do want to point out that I feel this is just a housekeeping bill. It will help the government solve some of its problems by putting the cost on to individuals, businessmen, and companies. There is no doubt about it, it is just another tax. It is a regressive tax. The business people and companies will not be pleased when they see what is going to happen to them. They may not understand it now, but they will certainly understand it when they see how much it is going to cost them. My friends from the NDP say-

subtopic: UNEMPLOYMENT INSURANCE ACT (1971) MEASURE TO ADD NEW CLASS OF INSURABLE EMPLOYMENT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I have been listening to the speeches made by a number of hon. members today. I get the impression-it may not be correct- that it is almost like having a free vote in the House; in our approach to the bill we tend to reflect the demography of our own constituencies. If it happens to be a highly labourintensive constituency where there is a lot of unemployment, then regardless of its geographical location we tend to reflect the specific problems of that constituency. I think this is admirable and I am not being critical.
We have heard in the House during the last few days speeches which reflect deep concern not just over Bill C-69 but over the whole approach we are making to social questions and social security. We have listened to hon. members who represent the wide open spaces in Alberta. We have listened to members who represent poor ridings, comparatively speaking, in Atlantic Canada, and we have heard them almost crossing party lines in terms of philosophy. I shall not mention any hon. member specifically but I am very impressed by this kind of scattered approach which expresses the attitudes of individual members concerned about the effects of a bill such as Bill C-69. There are extremes in this country which cross party lines.
As for myself, Mr. Speaker, I have no intention of crossing either parties or party lines this evening. I happen to represent a constituency which is primarily urban, primarily labour oriented. We are not experiencing high unemployment but we do find unemployment running close to the national figure. We have been through bad times; we have seen times much worse than they are at present.
Though in terms of social philosophy unemployment insurance is both desirable and necessary I must state at the outset, Mr. Speaker, that the Unemployment Insurance Commission is one of the most poorly managed of all federal government agencies. I suggest without equivocation that the commission and its regional and branch offices have displayed an inordinate propensity to err, to be disrespectful toward claimants, and at times to show an almost total disregard for people's sensitivities at a time of financial crisis.
I believe the state has a moral obligation to assist those citizens who are temporarily out of work due to sickness, a lay-off, pregnancy, or any other reasonable cause. We must always bear in mind that those who claim unemployment
November 4, 1975

insurance benefit are not those who exert any real influence on our economy. It is not they who make the major decisions, or blunders, in the Ministry of Finance or in the boardrooms of our major corporations. It is not they who manipulate the economy, who cause the peaks and lows in the business cycles. It is not they who control our trade policies or the amount of money in circulation. They are the victims of "the system", not the managers or administrators of it.
One constantly hears of the big UIC rip-off. One is constantly told of the terrible waste in financial and human terms caused by unemployment insurance, that it contributes to the desire to get something for nothing and that it is anti-work oriented. In fact, Mr. Speaker, most Canadians would rather work than draw UIC benefits, as I believe hon. members who talk to their constituents at week-ends will confirm. In the second place, such benefits are not excessive.
If a family man budgets on an income of $180 a week and suddenly finds himself without a pay cheque, he is in trouble. The average Canadian family cannot last longer than three weeks without income before having to dip into savings. If the head of the family has to wait four or five weeks, he is in a state of financial crisis. When he does get his UIC cheque, the current rate of about $120 is a far cry from the $180 I mentioned before. His whole budget is upset, and debts begin to pile up. Therefore I do not subscribe to the school of thought which believes that UIC benefits are excessive or counter productive.
It is true that a small proportion of claimants deliberately take advantage of the system, but there are con artists to be found on every street corner across Canada as well as in the boardrooms of our corporations. I am not condoning their behaviour. Those guilty of abuses should be severely dealt with, but let us not condemn the concept of unemployment insurance because a very small minority abuse it.
I should like to refer to an article which appeared in the Globe and Mail of February 21, 1975, entitled "U.I.C Called Poor Employer in Consultant's Report: Workers are inadequately informed and motivated." The newspaper story describes the report as saying that the Unemployment Insurance Commission is a poor employer and that most employees were "defensive, negative and poorly motivated". If this report is not accurate it is certainly the impression that most claimants get on entering a UIC office to discuss a problem with the staff. I use this word in a general sense, but I am old enough to have travelled a great deal on our railway system in this country, and in my opinion many UIC employees take the old CNR attitude that the public are second class citizens, and "If you don't like the system, get lost and don't bother us."

speechtext:
My friend says that is the CPR attitude and perhaps that is so. It is true that some people love to attack the government by verbally assaulting those civil servants closest to them, in this case UIC employees. None the less these employees should be emotionally mature enough to meet the public, even a hostile public at times.
Unemployment Insurance Act
Moreover, they should be able to give out information without adding to a series of contradictions, and without always being able to hide behind the vicissitudes of that infernal computer. It would seem that it is always the computer at fault, never the programmer.
As far as motivation is concerned, I find it difficult to understand why UIC employees are not happy in their work. They are well paid compared to private industry, they work in nice clean surroundings protected from the public by movable walls and jungles of plants, and they are usually falling all over each other because of overstaffing. What more could anyone want?

speechtext:
A typically Liberal example, not socialist. The consultant's report also stated that in all the thousands of words written and spoken about the Unemployment Insurance Commission there does not appear to exist a cogent and coherent statement of the objectives and policy of the commission. Even the new act of 1971 setting up the commission fails to make a definitive statement. The act does not deal with the principles which underlie the legislative and regulatory pronouncements.
It could be this glaring weakness that has led some of the public to look upon unemployment insurance as a kind of handout or welfare program, whereas in fact it is a compulsory contributory insurance program to protect working Canadians against loss of income due to unemployment.
The report also stated that the bulk of employees are confused and uncertain about society's perception of the value of the work they are trying to do. One cause of this, I am convinced, is the breakdown in communication between the UIC and claimants as a result of having to attempt to provide personalized service in a basically computerized constructed vacuum. The result of all this, Mr. Speaker, is that there is a constant turnover of staff. Moreover, there is little commitment on the part of UIC staff to do the best they can for their clients-not their slaves but their clients-who in many cases are looked upon as mere nuisances.
It is small wonder then that the average claimant has one hell of a time getting information from his local or branch UIC office. Usually the claimant gets no information, or inaccurate information. The claimant becomes bitter and frustrated. This in turn leads to bitterness among the UIC staff. And so the situation gets worse.
There are, however, staff members who are dedicated and knowledgeable, but unfortunately most of these are not accessible to the average claimant. I would, therefore, strongly recommend that the Unemployment Insurance Commission make available properly trained staff at all levels of its operations, particularly those dealing directly with claimants. After all, this is the front line. If people are to receive not only a fair deal from the UIC but are to feel that they have received a fair deal, it is incumbent upon the Unemployment Insurance Commission to make sure that their best trained people deal with claimants or clients in a very intelligent, acceptable, and humane way.
Another aspect of the Unemployment Insurance Commission that has given me serious concern is the position,
8862

November 4, 1975
Unemployment Insurance Act
responsibilities, and activities of the benefit control officers, in rural areas of Canada sometimes referred to as the "local Gestapo". This group was originally set up to provide claimants with information and guidance in searching for employment. The basic responsibility to date, however, has been to ensure that payments are made to bona fide claimants. This has led to all kinds of problems.
Benefit control officers, by and large, seem to have adopted the attitude that most claimants are guilty unless they can prove otherwise. For example, a claimant goes to a UIC office for what is called an interview with a benefit control officer, but for what is really a very subtle interrogation. The benefit control officer asks all kinds of leading questions and then summarizes his findings in the form of a statement in his own words. Claimants are not warned of the impact the statement will have. Moreover, a person in some cases is being asked to incriminate himself, something which runs counter to our basic concept of the common law.
Often the benefit control officer's report does not reflect the interview but, rather, his interpretation of the interview. It is also interesting to note that in 1972 and 1973 many retired policemen were hired as benefit control officers. That, by implication, speaks for itself.
Benefit control officers for the most part do not assist in directing claimants to job opportunities, which was the original reason they were engaged as members of the staff of UIC offices. They are really just "cops" chasing "crooks". As a result of this situation, I recommend that claimants be accompanied by representatives during all interviews and that claimants also be told before the interview the full meaning, impact, and consequences of the interview. Claimants should simply not be forced to sign interpretative statements of a self-incriminating nature.
I made reference a few moments ago to con artists. There are some slick operators but very few people who know how to handle benefit control officers. I have personally talked over the telephone, as well as in person, to middle aged men and women not too well versed in the English language who have had interviews with benefit control officers. The benefit control officer says to them, "You understand what you are reading?" If they say no, he reads it to them. Many of these people come from Europe, and they sign their names to the statement. These people then come to my office on a Saturday morning or afternoon and I ask them whether the statement is really what they said. Or they have a friend knowledgeable of the English language, and when they get talking together they say it is not exactly what they said but that is what they were made to sign.
I am not saying that the benefit control officer said, "Thou shalt sign or go to jail", but the impression was at least left with these people that if they did not sign they would be in trouble. We have to look at this sort of thing very carefully. I realize that a few people are taking advantage of the UIC system, but there are also a lot of innocent people being led down the garden path.
I should like to suggest some other changes that I think should be introduced at this time to eliminate not only hardship but bad feeling on the part of many claimants. I have never been able to understand why the so-called normal or regular waiting period after termination of earn-

ings must be two weeks. I am now talking about a regular or a maternity claim, not a sickness benefit claim. Surely in this computerized age one week would be sufficient. I do not understand why the waiting period has to drag on for two weeks, and then a claiment has to wait another two or three weeks afterwards.
Another aspect of the Unemployment Insurance Act which has not been altered relates to severance and vacation pay, and I think this is an injustice particularly to those in the construction industry. As hon. members know, vacation and severance pay are work credits earned during the claimant's employment, not when he is unemployed, and this money should not be classified as earnings after layoff. That simply is not fair. The construction trades in particular are badly hit. Most of this work is seasonal and subject to many layoffs. Since that is usually when they begin looking for new work, they are caught in the vicious circle of not having a vacation and having their vacation credits wiped out by the Unemployment Insurance Commission. Surely a more equitable and reasonable system can be worked out.
Another source of problems is the artificial division that took place some ten years ago, and this has been mentioned by other hon. members, when the old National Employment Service was separated into the Unemployment Insurance Commission and Canada Manpower. I suggest this arbitrary division has, for the most part, weakened the function of both agencies.
On the one hand the Unemployment Insurance Commission, in close consultation with claimants, is unable to place the claimant and tends to become punitive in its approach if the claimant remains unemployed for any length of time. On the other hand, Canada Manpower, though it often fails to find employment for its clients on UIC benefits, acts as a spy, surreptitiously passing on information to unemployment insurance officials, or benefit control officers, for punitive action by the Unemployment Insurance Commission. This situation obviously gives both agencies a very poor image in the community. This specific kind of relationship is also highly questionable and unfair.
Quite frankly I have found very few employers or employees who are satisfied with the present division between Canada Manpower and the Unemployment Insurance Commission. In fact I have not found very many employers or employees who have any use for Canada Manpower at all, but that is beyond the purview of this act.
Another aspect of this lack of fairness stems from the fact that the unemployment insurance offices receive information from Canada Manpower that "X" number of jobs are available in any given community. The Unemployment Insurance Commission then uses this information to disqualify claimants even though the UIC really has no idea where the jobs are, or what type of jobs are available. I recommend that the Unemployment Insurance Commission and Canada Manpower stop living common law and get married, or get married again.
I would now like to look at some of the proposed amendments introduced by the minister at first reading in July, and about which he spoke last week. I disagree completely
November 4, 1975

with the extension of the penalty period from three weeks to six weeks. That arbitrary extension results in an eight-week waiting period for those who quit employment voluntarily without just cause, and for those who refuse suitable employment, or who are dismissed for misconduct.
Just how is one to define "just cause" and "suitable employment"? This amendment could, and in many cases probably will, turn benefit control and insurance officers into petty local tyrants. There are many valid reasons why people leave employment voluntarily. There are also many valid reasons why people must refuse a specific job. What will be the yardstick, and what will be the criteria?
It is fair to say that most employees are pretty reasonable people, but you will always find personality clashes and conflicts in large plants, and even in small plants, between a worker and a foreman or, in a construction gang, between a labourer and a straw boss. If this conflict is of a personal nature the employee is at the mercy of the straw boss, the foreman, or the superintendent, and under the terms of this amendment he is in real trouble. If the job has become intolerable for him on a personal basis, let alone because of working conditions, what alternative does he have? He either sits back and takes it from the foreman or the employer, if that employer is not a reasonable man or woman, or he quits and is then penalized to the extent of six weeks instead of three, with another two weeks added, making it a total of eight weeks. This almost goes back to some of the old sweatshop days of years ago.
Let us not forget that 250,000 annual voluntary quits in the labour force represents only 2.5 per cent of the work force, and that 26,000 job refusals represents only two-tenths of 1 per cent of the labour force. This is certainly not "alarmingly high", as the minister suggested in his speech. The minister should know there are thousands of jobs today which are repugnant to most Canadians. Even he and his army of civil servants who drafted this legislation would find them unacceptable.
I realize that in some cases where a person is laid off and there is a job available, and if the individual is able to do that job, then that person should go back to work until something better comes along. However, when you have unemployment running at the rate of 7.2 per cent nationally, and from 15 per cent to 18 per cent in Atlantic Canada and in other parts, it is one thing to say you should go back to work and it is an entirely different thing to find a job in those parts of Canada.
Let us remember that this is a federal House of Commons. This is not the Alberta House, the British Columbia House, the Saskatchewan or Ontario House, this is the federal House. We are enacting federal legislation here and we are not just talking about those beautiful and wide open spaces of Alberta which I love. We are talking about heavily congested cities such as Montreal, Toronto, Vancouver, Halifax and so on. We are talking about the mining cities on Cape Breton Island. This is a federal House so let us not be too parochial in discussing a bill that affects all Canadians.
I would now like to look at the formula for financing the unemployment insurance program introduced in this bill. The minister said:
-it is now time to face practical needs for adjusting the application of
Unemployment Insurance Act
the financing methods and to bring them in line with current economic reality.
What is current economic reality? It is that since 1971 and the last amendments, or in fact since the new bill of June, 1971, the rate of unemployment has fallen below 5 per cent for only one month. The average since then has been 6.4 per cent in 1972, 6.3 per cent in 1973, 5.6 per cent in 1974, and at least 7 per cent this year.
The government by this amendment will face the practical needs not by reducing unemployment but by shunning its responsibilities, and making those who work pay for its bungling. In 1971 a threshold of 4 per cent unemployment was set as the level above which the government would assume the additional costs of UIC benefits. This would give the government incentive to fight unemployment. As we all know, this incentive was not good enough; now we find that the government has had to bear great financial responsibility for its lack of initiative and lack of ability to create enough jobs for enough people to reduce unemployment to acceptable levels.
The amendment would allow the benchmark to be adjusted each year on the basis of monthly unemployment rates over the last eight years. Extra costs would thus be borne by individuals.
High levels of unemployment have meant big payouts from UIC funds. Granted, this is not acceptable, but why should the working people of this country take the blame for it, for that is what this amendment virtually does? It is estimated that if unemployment reaches 7.6 per cent in 1976, as some predict, payments may reach $5 billion. What happens, for instance, if the anti-inflation program, so-called, drives unemployment up, as I am quite sure it will? Again it will be those least responsible who will have to bear the added cost through increased premiums.
What is probably most disturbing about this amendment is that the Liberals have said in effect that "normal unemployment" will now be considered to be 5.3 per cent, the average of the last eight years. Premiums will rise from approximately $1.40 per $100 insurable income to $1.60 or $1.70 per $100. However, and this is crucial, there is a ceiling on contributions. Thus, the UIC premium represents a bigger proportion of the income of lower paid workers than of higher paid workers. In effect this is another tax imposed on those on lower incomes. This is really what it amounts to, and those at the bottom pay a higher proportion of their insurable earnings for unemployment insurance.
I understand that my time is running out, Madam Speaker. When it comes to unemployment insurance, after being involved in it for four and one-half years I have come to the conclusion that these amendments-will really not amount to a hill of beans on the positive side, and on the negative side will make things worse for the lower paid employees. I call upon the minister to think a second time, and I call upon the members of the committee to whom this bill will be going to bring in meaningful amendments so that we will have some fairness and equity in respect of these amendments that will be commensurate with the needs, the demands, and ability to pay of the average Canadian.

speechtext:
Madam Speaker, as is the case with other members, over the last few years I have dealt with hundreds of cases involving unemployment insurance claims. Perhaps the most interesting was a claim that was turned down on the grounds of a pregnancy. It is interesting that this happened in such a place as Halifax-East Hants. Not since Adam gave birth to Eve has any man been pregnant, and yet this claimant was turned down on the ground of his pregnancy. There was no discrimination involved. The fact simply is that the young lady who punched the computer machine got the figure transposed.
After six days of debate I do not intend to cover a very wide range, but instead would like to bring to the attention of the House and the minister what I believe to be a discrimination against a small group of working people in Canada. These are Americans who have come to this country, have obtained work and have paid unemployment insurance premiums. Then, as happens in certain cases, they are not able to have their work permits renewed. The specific case I think of, occurred in respect of a young woman, a secretary at St. Mary's University in Halifax.
This young woman was supporting her husband who had come to this country as a student. He was also an American. Things went well until suddenly this summer she was refused an extension of her work permit. When she phoned the unemployment insurance office she was told she had made enough contributions to qualify for payments for a certain number of weeks, but when she went to collect it was a different story. She found that the payments were refused because she was not in a position to say she was available for work.
Physically she was available for work, and if a job had been offered and she had been in a position to take it she would have been working. But she had to advise the unemployment insurance office that she could not work because she did not have a permit to work in Canada. Here I believe we have an example of a very strict ruling being made. This woman was refused unemployment insurance payments because, although she had made all the necessary payments into the fund and her employer had as well, she could not obtain a permit to work.
This is the type of injustice I wish to bring as forcibly as I can to the attention of the minister. I hope the minister, when he appears before the committee and examines this case, will determine whether there is a remedy. I should like to say to the Minister of Manpower and Immigration (Mr. Andras), and to the officials of the Unemployment Insurance Commission who read these proceedings, that it is possible that the ruling made against this American woman in Halifax was a local ruling, and was inspired by some Philadelphia lawyer who had temporarily taken up residence in Halifax and had construed the law in a very strict and discriminatory sense. He went by the strict letter of the law, rather than by the intent of parliament or by anything that would represent common sense.
It is possible that the person advising the Unemployment Insurance Commission office in Halifax made a very strict and wrongful interpretation of the law which would not apply in other parts of Canada. If this is the case and the minister so advises me, I will give him the name of the young woman. She has now returned to the United States.

Perhaps they could send her at least her payments, or the money she paid into the unemployment insurance fund in good faith.
That is one way of looking at it. It may just have been a local error. If it is not, may I suggest two approaches to the minister. The first is that the young woman in her predicament be treated exactly the same as a person in the final year of work before going out on pension or retirement, that is, if she is over age 65 she cannot collect. Surely some method will have to be found so that those people do not have to pay into the unemployment insurance fund. After all, it is an insurance fund and one should pay in only if there is a reasonable probability that, certain circumstances having happened, one would receive payment or compensation for what he or she is trying to insure against. That is one aspect of it.
The other is that if the Department of Manpower is to give work permits to Americans and force them to pay into the unemployment insurance fund, then I think simple justice requires that if those people are put out of work through no fault of their own but through the fault of a change in government policy in Canada, they should receive unemployment insurance payments. I think that would have been the just result in respect of this young woman of whom I speak this evening. There it is. I hope the minister and the officials of the Unemployment Insurance Commission will put their heads together and come up with a solution to achieve justice for a small but important class of people.

subtopic: UNEMPLOYMENT INSURANCE ACT (1971) MEASURE TO ADD NEW CLASS OF INSURABLE EMPLOYMENT
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I am pleased tonight to have the opportunity to speak in this debate. I come from the province of Alberta, where there are not that many people unemployed. In fact often we are looking for skilled and unskilled people to help us out in the agricultural and energy fields. However, I have a number of problems, just as other members have, which I should like to take the opportunity tonight to bring to the attention of the House and the minister.
Many of my colleagues have spoken and have very clearly outlined many of the criticisms that can be levelled at the unemployment insurance bill. I do not mean to repeat what has been said because these criticisms have been very well set out. I am concerned about some of the measures that are being proposed, especially those aimed at the so-called low-income claimants and people over 65 years of age. Several positive and constructive suggestions have been brought forward. I hope the minister will look at them with a favourable eye and, as well, will look at some of the constituency problems that bother a great many of us constantly and which should be solved by some adequate amendments to the act.
Before discussing certain aspects of the bill I should like to pinpoint another problem which is of great concern to me. As I travel through my riding, and even throughout Canada, I come across a great many people who are discouraged with the Unemployment Insurance Act. They constantly say it is really only another welfare program. This concerns me because unemployment insurance is insurance against unemployment, and we should have an act which pertains to that element only. I should like to see
November 4, 1975

changes made so that we really do have a program of unemployment insurance that can stand on its own feet.
Assuming that the concept behind this program is insurance against unemployment, I should like to examine the situation which was described many times before but which I think bears repetition and which occurs in rural ridings. My riding of Westaskiwin is essentially rural. It contains some 30 to 40 communities numbering from around 600 people to around 5,000 people each. People working in these areas pay unemployment insurance, yet when they apply for unemployment insurance benefits when they lose their jobs they find they are often disentitled because of the so called distance rules. Let me give some examples.
I have had many complaints from communities in the Drayton Valley and Winfield areas in my constituency, some 85 miles from Edmonton. A man living in this area who becomes unemployed and applies for unemployment insurance often cannot find another job in that area, and if he does not state that he will take a job in Edmonton, 85 miles away and 170 miles round trip, he is disentitled. The commission justifies its decision by claiming that the individual concerned has limited himself to seeking work in an area where no opportunities for employment exist. And we call this an unemployment insurance program!
I would suggest to the minister that perhaps we could amend the act so that it would place a limit on the mile radius within which employment could be sought, say, for example 40 or 50 miles which would be the outside distance within which an individual must travel to work. If he cannot find a job within that area and if the only job for him is available some 100 or 200 miles away, some assistance should be given to that man in order to enable him to move himself and his family to another location nearer his work. This is important, and it is a matter which many hon. members representing rural ridings have been bringing up time and time again. It appears that there is certainly a problem here.
I am a member of parliament who perhaps does not have as many people calling me about unemployment insurance problems as do a great many of my colleagues, and I feel I am fortunate because in my riding a great many people can find work because they are close to the city of Edmonton. But there is the periphery area to which I referred which is having problems with the commission.
Another complaint that I receive fairly often is from a person who receives unemployment insurance while he is actively attempting to find work and, for some reason or another, finds he has been disentitled and then is asked to pay back in a lump sum what he has received. I agree that mistakes can be made, but it would seem fair for some type of payment program to be worked out so that this person is enabled to pay back the unemployment insurance which has been overpaid.
I have had cases of people who, three weeks after they had paid back the money to the Unemployment Insurance Commission, were told there was a mistake, that they were entitled to the benefit, and were then put back on unemployment insurance. This is a serious administrative problem, and I think it could be corrected and the matter dealt with in a more humane manner in cases where a person is paid more than is justified and then is disentitled.
Unemployment Insurance Act
I have another problem which occurs in my riding and which I would like the minister to consider because it is one that causes me a great deal of concern. The town of Ponoka and the surrounding area are some 75 miles from Edmonton and 110 miles from Calgary, yet the way the boundaries are divided the people in Ponoka who have legitimate complaints against the Unemployment Insurance Commission must travel to Calgary to have their cases dealt with there. They are closer to Edmonton and they cannot understand why they have to go in the other direction to have their problems solved. I think this could be changed easily. It is a complaint that I would like to get off my chest. I see the minister nodding his head and I am happy about that.
I want to emphasize a point that has been made by the hon. member for Brant (Mr. Blackburn) and, I am sure, by other hon. members, regarding the fact that unemployment insurance and Manpower should be reunited. In Edmonton the Unemployment Insurance Commission is located in one building, and across the town, some 10 or 15 blocks away, the Manpower office is located. Perhaps it would be possible to have one file for every individual and in this way a great many of the problems and discrepancies could be solved.
In the rural constituencies many jobs are available on a seasonal basis, sometimes for only two or three weeks. Any one who has run a farm, a ranch, or a small business knows that many times in the year he could employ a person for a short period of time. At the present time an individual who is collecting unemployment insurance benefits and who is offered short-term work, say, for example, on a farm during the harvest season or in a small business, will not accept such employment because he knows that if it is for less than eight weeks he will subsequently be unable to claim unemployment insurance.
However, if one file were kept on a person, it might be possible for him to accept short-term work provided he is all the while, even while employed, actively seeking a permanent job. This type of incentive could be built into the act, and if the Manpower department and the Unemployment Insurance Commission were amalgamated the problem would be largely solved. It is a complaint that comes to me many times from rural areas where farmers cannot give a job to people who are on unemployment insurance or on welfare to help them out for a few weeks because of the fact that they would lose their benefits.
I realize that the argument has been put forward many times that we should ask a claimant to work for six weeks before he is entitled to benefits. At present the act says that he must work for eight weeks before being entitled, so the suggestion I am making would not fit in here, but I think it would be possible if that individual had one file for the two departments.
Now I would like to deal briefly with the amendments that have been proposed. It seems to me that we are spending a great deal of money on unemployment insurance. We should want to tighten up the regulations so that it is in fact an insurance program and so that we are not spending so much money on it, when really we should be finding employment for these people. When I look at the amendments I really do not see how we will accomplish that.

November 4, 1975
Unemployment Insurance Act
We are estimating that we will cut people who are over 65, and who are unemployed off unemployment insurance benefits. This will affect approximately 5,000 senior citizens. It is a minute group. It has been stated that this will only amount to a saving of $2 million or $3 million, and I am not sure that we are saving it on the backs of the right people. If these people want to work after they lose their jobs and are actively seeking employment, they should be entitled to unemployment insurance benefits.
The so-called reform directed at low income recipients will severely hit individuals in that group who have dependants. No differentiation is being made between people having different needs or different ascribed circumstances. Under the 75 per cent benefit rate individuals in this group could receive a maximum of $46.26. At the 66% per cent rate they will receive a maximum of $41.07. The intent of the proposal is therefore to achieve restraint by denying $5 per week to those who are unemployed and who are in the most need of financial assistance.
Before I conclude I wish to make one more point. This matter comes to mind often when we speak of unemployment insurance. It is about seasonal employees who make a great deal of money in a short time. There are many in Canada today who are employed in the construction business or in oil fields. There are many examples I could use, but these people earn $10,000, $12,000, $13,000, $20,000 in six, seven or eight months of the year. They are still eligible for unemployment insurance, and I think it would be easier for us to amend the act to make it necessary for a claimant to state the amount he has earned in a particular year. If it is over a certain figure he should be unable to collect unemployment insurance.
I think it would greatly help the people of Canada who are working and paying unemployment insurance to feel that the program is doing something for those who really need insurance against unemployment.
I hope the minister will be open to suggestions in the committee from all parties in order to tighten up this bill and make it an insurance program, and I know we will be helping him in any way we can.

In other words, it is not what has been done in these amendments, it is what the minister has failed to change which bothers me.

One of the complaints I receive from claimants and from the general public deals with the question of the minor attachment provision in the bill which allows an initial benefit period and then a re-establishment period. One of the problems here is that to the mind of the average claimant it is extremely difficult to figure out which benefit period he is in. I should think that no one except some re-established bureaucrat would understand what a reestablished claim is. The program should be made more simple and meaningful for the claimant, as well as lawyers, union representatives, and all the professionals who become involved in this program so intensively, and to some extent further complicate the program.
In my view the minor attachment provision is a complicated factor. I suggest to the minister that he give consideration to there being only one attachment period, a major period, but the amount of work a person has to put in in order to establish himself for benefits should be reduced.
The idea of two sections is counter productive in terms of incentive for those seeking employment. Let me give an example of someone who is on a minor attachment, and who is then laid off. If he takes a new job for less than six weeks he does not go back on benefits because he has not re-established himself under the provisions of this act. The difficulty is that a claimant who does not re-establish himself has no incentive to take anything but a permanent job. If he goes back to a job which looks as though it could be for less than six weeks, there is a tremendous temptation-although it is a violation of the act-on the part of that claimant not to take the job because he will destroy the prospect of future benefits under the program. It seems to me that serious consideration should be given by the minister to the question of the minor attachment.

subtopic: CANADIAN PACIFIC RAILWAY-LAY-OFF OF EMPLOYEES AT WINNIPEG-GOVERNMENT ACTION
CANADIAN PACIFIC RAILWAY-LAY-OFF OF EMPLOYEES AT WINNIPEG-GOVERNMENT ACTION
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, on Monday, October 20, four days before it happened, I raised a question in this House concerning the pending lay-off of CPR employees at the Weston shops in Winnipeg. On that occasion I put the question to the Minister of Transport (Mr. Lang), but in all frankness he told me that he had nothing to report. The lay-off actually took place that Friday evening, October 24, and my colleague, the hon. member for Winnipeg North (Mr. Orli-kow) and I were at a meeting of a couple of hundred of those employees in Winnipeg on Sunday, October 26.
I raised the question again on Monday, October 27. On that occasion I put my question to the Minister of Labour (Mr. Munro). I notice his parliamentary secretary is here tonight. I had hoped from the conversation I had with the Minister of Labour yesterday that he would be here, for he assured me that he regarded this as a serious question. If the parliamentary secretary is answering for him I hope he has an answer worthy of the minister.
The situation is a serious one. Some 760 workers in the CPR shops at Winnipeg were laid off on Friday night, October 24, for what could well be an indefinite period, and this at a time when we are being told that our railway equipment needs to be modernized, We get questions in the House such as the questions that came today about the lack of sufficient equipment to move stock in western Canada. On all counts it seems to us to make no sense at all to lay off railway workers at this time.
Some of us feel it is part of a squeeze play at which the CPR has been a past master for a great many decades. There are railway wage negotiations coming up. It looks to some of us as though the CPR is laying off employees in the hope it will have a case against a wage increase that is worth anything at all.
There are rumours or expectations that we will soon have the report of Dr. Noel Hall on railway pensions. I trust it will make recommendations for substantial
Adjournment Debate
improvements. No doubt the CPR is ready to say no before its officials even see the report. It is well known that the CPR is forever putting pressure on the government to provide it with money. I suppose it is not to be blamed for that because it has been getting money, land, mineral rights, and things like that from this country for a good many decades.
It is precisely because of what the CPR has got out of this country that we feel it has an obligation to provide proper and adequate railway service and that it has an obligation to play its part in maintaining our economy at a decent level.
A corporation like the CPR is not doing that when it lays off employees to the tune of 760, as happened in Winnipeg recently. I believe this may have happened, although not to the same extent, in Calgary and other cities in Canada and even to some extent in Montreal. My plea to the minister was that he indicate to the House what the government is going to do about this matter.
I started by indicating a couple of dates, namely, October 20 when I first raised the matter in the House this fall-we have in fact been raising it for months-and October 27 when I raised it again. Between those two dates the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) and the Minister of Labour were both at Winnipeg. They were met there by these employees who were about to be laid off and both of them assured the workers that they would look into the case to see what could be done. When I put that in as part of my question to the Minister of Labour on Monday, October 17, he agreed that what I said was correct, that he and the Prime Minister had met these men and had assured them they would see what could be done. They are still waiting for a reply.
I hope the Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Labour (Mr. Leblanc) can tell the House that the minister has taken up this matter with the Prime Minister and the Minister of Transport, and that the cabinet as a whole has become aware of the seriousness of the situation, and that he has something to say tonight that will be more hopeful news to these CPR employees at Winnipeg than the unemployment they are suffering at the present time.
