Madam Speaker, first it is important to reassure the hon. member and tell him that the Minister of Labour (Mr. Munro) is very much aware of the vital problem he has raised with his usual competence, and that he is quite concerned about the future of those CPR employees. For that reason, the minister has immediately set up a group of senior civil servants, as the Prime Minister himself had promised the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles). This group includes representatives from the Departments of Labour, Manpower and Immigration and Transport; it has undertaken a comprehensive study of that problem.
The group already met on Friday October 31, 1975, and is to meet again tomorrow Wednesday, November 5, 1975, as well as in the near future, as required. There is no doubt that the Minister of Labour will inform the hon. member and the House of the solutions recommended by this group of senior civil servants from the three departments mentioned.

November 4, 1975
Adjournment Debate

It is important to note that CP Rail have given written notice to each individual concerning the lay-off and have advised the minister of Labour accordingly. In all cases the employees have received lay-off notice in accordance with the terms of the collective agreement. Such terms, of course, provide for the lay-off of the person with the least seniority.
At one time the unions had alleged that CP Rail was in violation of the lay-off notice provisions in the Canada Labour Code. When this alleged violation was reported, officials of the Department of Labour met with the respective union leaders and it was ascertained that no violation of the lay-off notice provisions of the Canada Labour Code had taken place.

The minister apologizes for not being present tonight. As for the question of knowing whether the CPR is responsible for the dismissals, I cannot discuss it for the time being because I do not know all the circumstances surrounding them.

subtopic: CANADIAN PACIFIC RAILWAY-ALLEGED SCRAPPING OF FREIGHT CARS-REQUEST FOR INVESTIGATION
CANADIAN PACIFIC RAILWAY-ALLEGED SCRAPPING OF FREIGHT CARS-REQUEST FOR INVESTIGATION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, like my colleague, the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles), on October 29 I addressed a question to the Minister of Transport (Mr. Lang) with regard to lay-offs that had taken place several days earlier of some 760 CPR employees.
My colleague and I had raised this question a number of times earlier in the year because of the rumours and warnings of the lay-off of a substantial number of people with fairly long service. That is a large lay-off for one city. On each occasion that we raised this matter we were told by the minister that, first, he had no direct control over CPR and, second, that we had his assurance he would look into the question.
When it became obvious that more than 700 people had been given virtually permanent notice that they would no longer be employed by CPR, I started to look into the matter more intensively. It became obvious that the lay-off to a large extent was due to the CPR using hopper cars built on the order of and paid for by the Government of Canada. Because of the use of these hopper cars to move grain from western Canada to Thunder Bay or Vancouver, freight cars that had traditionally been used by the CPR were no longer being used.
It seems strange to me that the CP should be laying off several thousand people across the country while CN has laid off virtually nobody. This has been confirmed for me. As I say, it seems strange, since each railway carries about half of the grain which is transported.
The second question to which I addressed myself was whether in fact the government had made any arrangements when it decided to purchase hopper cars for use by both railways in moving grain-whether the government

had had any discussions with the railways and the Wheat Board as to who should own the cars, who should be responsible for their maintenance, and whether the railways had been asked to give any commitment that the hopper cars used to move grain would be in addition to the freight cars used until then. I found that not only had there been such discussions but that questions had been asked and that the minister then responsible for the Wheat Board has answered them in a positive fashion. I refer to a question put to the Minister of Transport (Mr. Lang) on May 29, 1972, by the former member for Regina East. The exchange was as follows:

subtopic: CANADIAN PACIFIC RAILWAY-ALLEGED SCRAPPING OF FREIGHT CARS-REQUEST FOR INVESTIGATION
speechtext: Can the minister indicate what assurances have been given by the railways that they will maintain their present quantity of rolling stock engaged in grain movement-

speakeroldname: Hon. Otto E. Lang (Minister of Justice):
speakerposition: Minister of Communications; Minister of Transport; Minister responsible for the Canadian Wheat Board
subtopic: CANADIAN PACIFIC RAILWAY-ALLEGED SCRAPPING OF FREIGHT CARS-REQUEST FOR INVESTIGATION
speechtext:
It would be very much the purpose and intention of the government to make sure that the hopper cars put into use in this fashion are additional to other rolling stock made available for the movement of grain.
Then the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Stanfield) asked a supplementary question:
Am I to infer from the minister's answer that to date, at least, the railways have given no commitment that these hopper cars will be in addition to existing equipment and that the equipment now in use will be maintained?
To which the minister replied:
No, Mr. Speaker, the Leader of the Opposition is quite incorrect in thinking that. The railways have had very firm discussions with the Canadian Wheat Board on the amount of rolling stock they have available which is to be dedicated to grain. These 2,000 hopper cars will be additional to that rolling stock.
We find now that this agreement has not been lived up to. Of course there is a reduction in the amount of freight which CP is moving, but the CP is destroying up to ten boxcars a day, many of them in very good condition. I say that the CP, unlike the CN, has not lived up to its agreement with the Government of Canada and I call on the minister to take action to ensure that the CP ceases this wanton destruction of very useful equipment which it is scrapping simply because it suits it to use the hopper cars and not to use the equipment it promised the minister it would continue to use. It is because of this misuse of authority that 750 people have been laid off. I think the minister could, and should, take action.

speakeroldname: Mr. Ralph E. Goodale (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Transport):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Transport
subtopic: CANADIAN PACIFIC RAILWAY-ALLEGED SCRAPPING OF FREIGHT CARS-REQUEST FOR INVESTIGATION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in 1974 when there was a serious shortage of grain cars the federal government agreed to pay part of the cost of upgrading and repairing of, I believe, 2,400 cars for grain service. This aid was given on the understanding, contained in the agreement, that the removal of regular cars could not be accelerated. The agreement is being adhered to by both railway companies. I am informed by CP that of the cars affected by this agreement only two have been scrapped- they had both been involved in major accidents and repairs in each case would have been extremely uneconomical.
The hon. member referred specifically to a problem in Winnipeg. CP Rail does not scrap cars which are in good condition. He referred to the situation involving the purchase of hopper cars. Of course the justification purchase by the government of some 4,000 new hopper cars, now being delivered, was largely based on the inability of the railways to provide capital for hopper car replacement.
November 4, 1975

I have been assured by Canadian Pacific that the scrapping program for boxcars in Winnipeg has involved basically boxcars 35 years of age or more and which are requiring extensive maintenance. It is more economical to take them out of service than to maintain them with constant and expensive repairs. This is the normal program that is also being pursued by Canadian National.
With respect to the matter of lay-offs, I know the hon. member will have heard the comments of the Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Labour (Mr. Leblanc) indicating our concern for the problem and our present attention to it. As the Minister of Transport (Mr. Lang) pointed out to the hon. member in his reply earlier in the House, the lay-off situation affecting the railways is in part due to the slowdown in the economy and a resultant modification in the use of cars. This sometimes means fewer maintenance forces to keep the fleet operative. The railways are forced to lay off where services are no longer required. It is apparent that the situation is a difficult one, but even under present circumstances the railways are able to satisfy the unusually high target for grain movement that they have been set this year by the Canadian Wheat Board.

subtopic: OLYMPIC GAMES-LIMITATION OF CONSTRUCTION CONTRACTS TO QUEBEC COMPANIES-GOVERNMENT ACTION TO ELIMINATE DISCRIMINATION

speakeroldname: Mr. A. D. Alkenbrack (Frontenac-Lennox and Addington):
subtopic: OLYMPIC GAMES-LIMITATION OF CONSTRUCTION CONTRACTS TO QUEBEC COMPANIES-GOVERNMENT ACTION TO ELIMINATE DISCRIMINATION
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I rise tonight to debate, not for the first time, a question pertaining to fair play for all Canadians. On October 28 I asked a simple question of the government House leader in his capacity as Acting Prime Minister. I asked if the government planned to investigate the allegations that only firms having their principal place of business in Quebec were allowed to bid on projects at the Olympic site in Montreal. The Acting Prime Minister (Mr. Sharp) replied that the government did not have administrative responsibility for the Olympic projects.
That answer is unacceptable, Madam Speaker, both to me and to the Canadian people. When the Olympic financing bill was before the federal parliament this House passed a bill allowing the federal government to advance a considerable amount of money from the federal treasury to enable COJO, the Olympic organizing committee, to get started. That same bill authorized the post office to issue a continuing series of Olympic stamps. Part of the proceeds from the sale of those stamps has been turned over to COJO. The bill also authorized the Royal Canadian Mint to strike seven sets of Olympic coins. Part of the proceeds from the sale of these Olympic coins is also turned over to COJO, and I might add that these stamps and coins are sold in every province of Canada and the two territories.
Moreover, there is an Olympic lottery in operation, where for $10 Canadians in all parts of the land can take a chance on becoming an instant millionaire. Here too, the tickets on the lottery are sold everywhere in Canada, not just in Montreal, and not just in the province of Quebec.
The mayor of Montreal tells us on frequent occasions that the sale of stamps and coins and Olympic lottery tickets will cover the cost of the Olympics, and that this will not be a repeat of the 1967 world's fair in Montreal
Adjournment Debate
when the Canadian people picked up the deficit for the fair. Madam Speaker, I do not believe this.
We know already that the 1976 Olympics will incur an enormous deficit, and we have already heard figures of the deficit that run as high as half a billion dollars. Be that as it may, Madam Speaker, the fact of the matter is that the Canadian people have been sold a bill of goods, that Canada is the host of the 1976 Olympics, and that the cost of the games should be borne by all Canadians.
Let us pursue the matter of the Canadian Olympic Games a step further and take up the question of security. We are told that several thousand men and women from the Canadian armed forces will be assigned to the Olympic site in Montreal and to other areas as part of the security arrangements for the games. In addition, the Department of Justice and the Solicitor General's department will be involved in security for the games, including the assigning of thousands more people from the Royal Canadian Mounted Police and the immigration service.
It begins to look as though the tail is certainly wagging the dog in the matter of the games, if in fact the federal government is not in any way involved in the administration of them. As I mentioned earlier, I do not accept that as the truth, nor do the rest of the people of Canada who are paying the cost of the 1976 extravaganza.
In spite of the fact that the province of Quebec changed the name of its provincial legislature to the national assembly, it is no less a province of Canada than is Ontario, and Quebec is no more a sovereign state than the province of Ontario. If Quebec is a sovereign state, Madam Speaker, perhaps the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) can tell us how any foreign state can enter into international agreements that involve the armed forces of Canada, the Royal Canadian Mounted Police, the Royal Canadian Mint, the Canadian Post Office, or strike-bound, rather what is left of it, and the other federal departments that are presently involved in the 1976 Olympic Games in one way or another.
The tendering regulations employed by COJO were not drawn up by that corporation. They are provincial regulations, and that means that the province of Quebec does not recognize the right of companies having their main offices in Ontario or other provinces to pour cement at the Olympic site, or to sell furniture to the games committee, or to have any meaningful, gainful part to play in the construction or outfitting of the Olympic facilities.
In other words, we are expected to pay for the Games and we are encouraged to help pay for the Games not only by the Olympic Games committee, the province of Quebec, and the city of Montreal, but by the federal government. However, we in other provinces should not expect to be allowed to bid on any Olympic projects. Bidding is restricted to companies having their principal place of business in the province of Quebec, and we are told that this is right and proper since the federal government is not responsible for the administration of the Games. This is the Trudeau just society. This attitude on the part of the federal government cannot be condoned.
We are entitled to a better answer than the one offered by the government House leader. This "hands off" attitude

November 4, 1975
Adjournment Debate
was reflected in the federal government's refusal to convene a full-scale investigation into the allegations of fraud in the letting of contracts for the first phase of construction at the Olympic site. I ask, in the name of my constituents, how long does the federal government intend to keep silent on the appalling mismanagement of the Olympic Games administration?
The matter of discrimination against Canadian contractors and suppliers outside Quebec by the Olympic Games committee is only a part of the broad question of mismanagement of the Olympic Games administration, and I suggest that the federal government cannot get off the hook simply by stating that it is not responsible for the administration of the Games.
When we debated the Olympic financing bill we were told by members on all sides of the House that the 1976 Olympic Games would be a sort of catalyst to draw Canadians closer together, sharing the burden of getting the games site ready and sharing in the honour and glory of the best Olympic Games ever. Because of the administration of the Olympic Games it has had the opposite effect. It has had a divisive effect, fed by the greed of Quebec contractors and suppliers, the deceptive impostures of Liberalism, and by the high and mighty attitude of COJO officials and political figures in the province. I am asking for a more suitable answer to my question of October 28, Madam Speaker, and I will continue repeating my question until I do get a plausible answer to this enigma
which deprives the majority of Canadian contractors of their basic rights.

speakeroldname: Mr. Lloyd Francis (Parliamentary Secretary to President of the Treasury Board):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the President of the Treasury Board
subtopic: OLYMPIC GAMES-LIMITATION OF CONSTRUCTION CONTRACTS TO QUEBEC COMPANIES-GOVERNMENT ACTION TO ELIMINATE DISCRIMINATION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the hon. member has asked questions in this House relating to which firms are being invited to bid on construction contracts at the Olympic site in Montreal. On October 28 the Acting Prime Minister, (Mr. Sharp) stated that the federal government does not have administrative responsibility for the Olympic projects.
Furthermore, in answer to questions from members of this House, the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) has restated the position of the federal government, in that it would not pick up any possible deficit on the Olympic Games, and that the federal government has not been asked to do so by either the province of Quebec or the city of Montreal. We, therefore, have no involvement in these construction activities.
Construction on the Olympic site is the responsibility of the city of Montreal. It is the city which is responsible for the tender calls and the allocation of contracts which are monitored by the province of Quebec.
It is true, I might add, that aid has been extended to the Games through legislation of this House relating to the stamp program, the Olympic coins program, and others, but the terms of that legislation do not permit the Government of Canada to supervise or intervene in the process of tendering on the Olympic site.
Motion agreed to and the House adjourned at 10.25 p.m.
